strategy_name: 2% Rule + 6% Rule + Iron Triangle sizing
mechanism: percent-capped dollar risk per trade and a monthly equity heat cap prevent ruin and force a cooling-off review
setup_summary: Maximum dollar risk per trade is 2% of account equity, and that 2% must also absorb slippage and commissions (Iron Triangle: total acceptable dollar risk / risk-per-share from entry to stop = maximum position size). If realized plus open-trade losses for the month reach 6% of month-start equity, stop trading for the rest of the month, review the system, and return next month at reduced size, scaling back up only after performance goals are met.
trigger_invalidation: Not a market-timing rule; the ceiling recomputes each month from month-start equity — profits are not counted against the 6% heat cap, only realized losses and amounts at risk in open trades.
risk_geometry: Entry: per trade; stop: defined per trade, the rule sizes so that (entry - stop) x size <= 2% equity including costs; hard lifecycle cap: 6% monthly equity drawdown stops all trading for the month; after a severe drawdown, lower the risk fraction and increase size in steps.
quote: The 2% Rule dictates your maximum dollar risk per trade. Two percent of a $28,000 account is $560, which must cover not only your risk but also slippage and commissions.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 9 (Risk Management), Q 9-4, 9-8, 9-12, 9-14 to 9-17; Afterword (monthly 6% stop)
notes: Book asserts these rules are 'proven by experience' (Q 9-6: never meet a margin call, never average down, first mistake is cheapest, liquidate worst position first). The 2% per-trade cap and 6% monthly stop map directly onto V8's RiskGate deterministic admission and heat cap; the 6% monthly rule is a lifecycle_rule candidate. Book also warns stops can gap (Answer 9-11) and that leverage (futures margins as low as 5%, Answer 8-10) makes these caps mandatory.

strategy_name: Impulse system (EMA + MACD-Histogram censorship filter)
mechanism: agreement between market inertia (EMA slope) and market power (MACD-Histogram slope) defines a directional censorship regime
setup_summary: Compute the slope of a fast EMA (market inertia) and the slope of the last two bars of MACD-Histogram (market power). Both rising -> green, shorting prohibited; both falling -> red, buying prohibited; contradictory slopes -> blue, both directions permitted. Used as a censorship/regime gate, not an automatic entry system: its best signals come when the red or green color disappears (e.g., red turning non-red completes a double bottom and suggests buying; green disappearing near the end of an upswing suggests taking profits).
trigger_invalidation: The filter flips when either slope changes sign; the book explicitly warns that automating the color-consistent states produces multiple whipsaws (e.g., between bars C and G in Q 7-12), so the actionable signal is the disappearance of red/green, not sustained color.
risk_geometry: Not an entry-timing system; a gate only. Entries are taken with other tools within the permitted direction; no stop/target specified by the system itself.
quote: The primary role of the Impulse system is not to tell traders when to buy or sell. Rather, it shows them when they're prohibited from buying or shorting.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 7 (Trading Systems), Q 7-10 to 7-13; Answers 7-10, 7-11, 7-12
notes: Fully price-derived (EMA slope + MACD-Histogram slope), so directly computable on BTCUSDT 1h perp data. For V8 this is a regime/censorship filter candidate rather than an expert: it could gate which directions existing experts may emit, matching the book's framing. Key methodological caveat from the book: the sustained-color states whipsaw if automated; only the disappearance of red/green is a clean signal - so it should be wired as a state-transition filter, not a level filter.

strategy_name: Multi-indicator independent confirmation gate
mechanism: No single indicator is reliable; requiring two or more independent signal families to agree raises the hit rate of reversal timing, and contradiction between equally strong indicators is itself actionable (do not act).
setup_summary: The book's central thesis, stated repeatedly: every signal (price pattern, candlestick, volume, oscillator) must be confirmed by an independent indicator before acting. Rules: (1) do not act when two equally strong indicators contradict; (2) weight the stronger indicator; (3) wait for a third confirming indicator when signals conflict. Confirmation can also be continuation confirmation (do not exit a valid trend) — the book treats false exits as a first-order failure mode.
trigger_invalidation: N/A — this is a methodology invariant, not a trade trigger; its falsifiable component is the claim that confirmed signals fail less often, which V8 can test by comparing episode outcomes with vs without cross-feature-group confirmation.
risk_geometry: none — a candidate-generation gate: emit CandidateDraft only when the primary trigger is corroborated by an independent feature group (e.g., candlestick + volume + response), and suppress emission when two equally strong groups disagree.
quote: No signal provides enough by itself to act upon with confidence. Always seek confirmation before you act.
chapter_anchor: Part 8 (entire part: 'why is confirmation the key process'); Part 1 Seg 2
notes: Directly relevant to V8's candidate-generation contract: the book's confirmation discipline maps to requiring cross-feature-group confluence in MarketState before CandidateDraft, and 'contradiction -> do not act' maps to an explicit suppression rule. The book repeatedly documents strong confirmed signals that failed anyway (eBay, Kraft, Wal-Mart), which is itself the evidence for V8's stance that no gate removes falsification risk.

strategy_name: Per-trade account risk cap (5% max)
mechanism: Bounding per-trade risk keeps a single adverse move from destroying the account under leverage; offered leverage (50:1) is not a target
setup_summary: Never risk more than 5% of the account on any one trade (the book's hard line: 'risking anything greater than 5 to 10 percent of your account on any one trade is financial suicide'). Even at modest 10:1 leverage a 10% adverse move wipes the account, so position size must be derived from stop distance and account equity, not from the leverage offered.
trigger_invalidation: N/A - permanent risk rule.
risk_geometry: Position size = (risk percent x equity) / stop distance; margin is not a loss cap; margin-call behavior (broker closes positions) must be modeled.
quote: Professional traders who survive in the forex market will usually not risk more than 5 percent of their account on any one trade, and using stops can be a good way to limit the downside risk of leverage.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'Leverage' and 'Margin'; Chapter 11, Mistake #8
notes: Crypto perp leverage (commonly 25x-125x) makes this cap more load-bearing than in spot FX; complements the V8 heat cap and one-exposure rule. The book's margin-call description (broker force-closes when equity falls below maintenance margin) is a simulator cost-model input.

strategy_name: Break-even stop promotion at +1R
mechanism: once the position has moved in favor by the full initial risk distance, promoting the stop to entry removes tail risk from the winner while leaving the upside intact
setup_summary: As soon as a position has profited by the same amount that was initially risked (1R), move the stop-loss to break-even; some traders also close a partial position at that point. This is an exit-management rule layered on any entry.
trigger_invalidation: Only triggers after price reaches +1R in favor; the original structural stop remains in force before that level.
risk_geometry: Stop promoted from initial stop_r to entry at +1R; target_r unchanged; a standard lifecycle transition on the existing expert's frozen references.
quote: A good habit of more successful traders is to employ the rule of moving your stop to break even as soon as your position has profited by the same amount that you initially risked through the stop order.
chapter_anchor: Section 08, Risk management (trailing stops / break-even)
notes: A canonical lifecycle rule, implementable in src/v8/lifecycle.py for existing experts (trend_pullback, failed_breakout, liquidity_sweep_reclaim) with no new features; perp leverage makes the risk-free-trade property especially valuable. Companion guidance: trailing stops and partial position closure noted as alternatives.

strategy_name: Fixed-percent risk cap per trade (2% / rule of 1/6)
mechanism: capping per-trade risk as a small fraction of equity bounds drawdown so a single loss cannot erase prior profitability
setup_summary: Risk at most 2% of equity on any single trade (pros' consensus); a conservative variant caps risk at 1/6 of free capital when conviction is not complete. Position size = (equity * risk_fraction) / stop distance. The book ties this to survival statistics: 99% of day traders lose money and one oversized loss eliminates any winning streak.
trigger_invalidation: Cap applies unconditionally at admission; both percentages are variants of one sizing family.
risk_geometry: notional = (equity * risk_fraction) / stop_distance; maps directly to V8 RiskGate's heat cap with position size derived from stop_r.
quote: Pros recommend 1:2 risk-reward ratio, and not risking more than 2% of your equity on any single trade.

notes: Pure sizing rule, applies unchanged to BTCUSDT perps; particularly relevant given default high leverage. Companion leverage lesson: 'Using 1:50 leverage means that a 2% adverse move could wipe out all your equity' - book recommends effective leverage of 10:1 or less.

strategy_name: Minimum 1:2 risk-reward admission gate
mechanism: requiring target at least 2x the stop filters out low-expectancy entries before capital is committed
setup_summary: Establish a risk-reward ratio for every trade and admit a candidate only if potential gain is at least 2x the amount willing to be lost (target_r >= 2 * stop_r); otherwise skip the entry as not worth the risk.
trigger_invalidation: Reject candidate when structure-based target yields reward/risk below 2:1.
risk_geometry: target_r >= 2 * stop_r, both derived from market structure rather than fixed pips.
quote: Generally, the risk-reward ratio should be at least 1:2, if not more. Having a solid risk-reward ratio can prevent traders from entering positions that ultimately are not worth the risk.
chapter_anchor: Section 08, Risk-reward ratio
notes: A pure risk-layer admission rule for V8's risk_geometry; applies unchanged to BTCUSDT 1h. Stated as a universal rule across strategies, not an empirical claim.

strategy_name: Coverage/neglect premium: value works best in lightly analyzed names; earnings-based cheapness stays robust in large caps
setup_summary: Mispricing is more frequent among names too small to justify analyst coverage, so simple value screens find more bargains there; in the book's decile tests the smallest-cap group did NOT itself outperform (12.1% vs 11.9% for largest decile) - the outperformance comes from the value screen applied inside the universe, not from size alone. The Magic Formula stays discriminative in large caps (best-decile 18.88%/yr vs worst 4.66%, spread >14 pts) where price/book fails (low P/B best-vs-worst decile spread only ~2 pts among $1B+ names).
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: prefer a value/quality screen to locate bargains; expect concentration of bargains in low-coverage instruments. Invalidation: the coverage/neglect premium collapses if the market becomes fully efficient in the target universe (e.g., after broad retail/institutional adoption).
risk_geometry: n/a beyond the underlying value strategy - this is universe-selection guidance.
quote: companies that are too small for professionals to buy and that are not large enough to generate sufficient commission revenue to justify analyst coverage are more likely to be ignored or misunderstood. As a result, they are more likely to present opportunities to find bargain-priced stocks.
chapter_anchor: Appendix p.149-151
notes: If V8 ever expands beyond BTCUSDT, alt perps are the low-coverage analog - more mispricing but thinner liquidity (capacity check). strategy_name: Signal averaging: trailing-window inputs are noisy per name but informative across a portfolio
setup_summary: The Magic Formula deliberately uses trailing (last-year) earnings even though value depends on future earnings, because a noisy proxy becomes an unbiased average across 20-30 names: 'on average, last year's earnings will often provide a pretty good estimate for normal earnings going forward.' For the few who can project normal-year earnings 3-4 years out, 5-8 high-conviction names in different industries can replace the 20-30-name basket; for everyone else the diversified basket is mandatory.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: evaluate any per-name signal in aggregate across many candidates before judging it; a trailing-window feature that is weak per episode may still rank families well in aggregate. Invalidation: aggregation across too few candidates, or across a non-stationary universe, re-introduces per-name noise.
risk_geometry: n/a - aggregation/evaluation methodology for the lab.
quote: using last year's earnings is often a good indicator of what earnings will look like in the future. Of course, for individual companies, this may not be the case.

strategy_name: Phased portfolio entry + fixed-cycle rebalance (5-7 names every 2-3 months; replace only matured names)
setup_summary: To reproduce the tested average, do not buy the full 20-30-name portfolio at once: add 5-7 names every 2-3 months over the first ~9-10 months, then each cycle replace only the 5-7 names that reach the one-year holding mark with fresh top-ranked selections; stay committed for a minimum of 3-5 years regardless of results.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: enter the portfolio in tranches on a calendar schedule rather than all at once; exit names on a fixed holding cycle. Invalidation: the schedule assumes the average (not single-name) result, so deviating to concentrated timing or abandoning the cycle re-introduces timing luck.
risk_geometry: Entry in calendar tranches (every 2-3 months), each name held ~1 year, replaced on schedule; no price stop; risk governed by the schedule plus basket diversification.
quote: we will have to work into our magic formula portfolio over the course of our first year of investing. That means adding 5 to 7 stocks to our portfolio every few months until we reach 20 or 30 stocks in our portfolio.

strategy_name: 2% Rule — per-trade risk cap
mechanism: capping per-trade dollar risk as a fixed fraction of equity keeps a losing streak from breaching survival thresholds regardless of stop distance
setup_summary: Never risk more than 2% of account equity on any single trade, including commissions and slippage; position size = (2% x equity) / (risk per unit = entry − stop). Far stops force smaller size; tight stops allow larger size. When losing, keep size consistent or reduce it — never increase size to recoup losses.
trigger_invalidation: A trade is rejected if its dollar risk (size x stop distance + costs) exceeds 2% of equity; reduce size to fit, or skip the trade.
risk_geometry: Entry/stop come from the method; size is derived so that risk <= 2% of equity; this is the admission gate applied to every trade.
quote: The 2% Rule, the most important rule of money management, protects you from ever losing more than 2% of your account equity on any single trade.
chapter_anchor: Money Management chapter, Answers 70-75, 81-82
notes: Maps directly to V8 RiskGate deterministic admission and position sizing. In high-leverage perp crypto, per-trade risk as a % of equity is the key scaling input and must respect the one-exposure-per-direction rule.

strategy_name: 6% Rule — monthly loss cap with hard stop for the month
mechanism: anchoring the heat budget to start-of-period equity and freezing new admissions once realized + open risk consumes the budget protects capital across consecutive losses
setup_summary: Record equity at the start of the month. If equity dips 6% below that level (realized losses plus risk on open trades), stop trading for the balance of the month. Total risk in open trades plus realized losses never exceeds 6% of start-of-month equity.
trigger_invalidation: Rule blocks new trades once month-to-date realized + open risk >= 6% of start-of-month equity; risk budget can only be freed by closing trades to breakeven/winning (moving stops to breakeven removes that trade from the risk pool).
risk_geometry: No entry/stop geometry — a period admission gate. Breakeven-stop moves free risk budget (trades C/D in Answer 78).
quote: To observe the 6% Rule, you must stop trading as soon as your equity dips 6% below that level. Stay out for the balance of the month.
chapter_anchor: Answers 77-80
notes: Refines V8's heat cap into a fixed period budget anchored at period start with a hard stop-for-period admission rule. In 24/7 crypto the 'month' is an arbitrary anchor — test calendar-month vs rolling-window variants. Companion lifecycle rule from the same chapter: 'We may move stops only in the direction of the trade, never against it.'
book: Come Into My Trading Room (Study Guide) 2002

strategy_name: Triple Screen — three-timeframe hierarchy (strategic/tactical/execution)
mechanism: higher timeframes set the strategic direction that trades on lower timeframes follow; conflicting signals across timeframes are filtered out rather than averaged
setup_summary: Make the strategic (bullish/bearish) decision on the highest timeframe, the tactical entry/exit decision on the middle timeframe, and execution on the lowest (weekly -> daily -> intraday, factor-of-five between timeframes). Filter conflicting signals between timeframes, keeping only aligned signals; combine one trend-following indicator group with oscillators so their messages are balanced.
trigger_invalidation: No trade when timeframes conflict; the method prescribes standing aside or reducing size on conflict. The strategic decision must be made before looking at the tactical chart.
risk_geometry: Methodology layer — no direct geometry; risk sizing still governed by the 2%/6% rules.
quote: If you work with weekly, daily, and intraday charts, then make your strategic decision... on the weekly chart, then tactical on the dailies, and find entry and exit points using intraday charts.
chapter_anchor: Answer 45; Answer 44 (factor-of-five); Answer 26
notes: V8 is single-timeframe (BTCUSDT 1h). The transferable lesson is the regime-filter pattern: higher-timeframe trend (e.g., 4h/1d EMA slope) as a gate on 1h expert admissions — a refinement candidate for trend_pullback's trend requirement. 24/7 crypto has no session boundaries, but bar aggregation is arbitrary (weekly-equivalent = 7x24h aggregation).
book: Come Into My Trading Room (Study Guide) 2002

strategy_name: 2-for-1 money management and swing-trade risk rules
mechanism: Skewed payoff (many small losses, few home runs) requires capping initial risk, banking partial profits at 1R, and protecting the remainder at breakeven so no single trade can be damaging
setup_summary: Protective stop on every trade, placed below the setup's lowest bar (longs) / above the highest bar (shorts), never risking more than 5% of price and ~2% of account. Once profit >= initial risk, sell half and move the remaining stop to breakeven (2-for-1). Then scale out further and trail below the lowest low of the prior two bars. Exit positions not profitable within 1-2 days; time-stop out by ~7 bars unless in a strong trend; take most of a parabolic move; never add to losers; if pyramiding, 3-2-1 ratio with largest position first.
trigger_invalidation: N/A - rules apply to every position. 'No tickie, no tradie': no entry without a confirmed trigger (never fade by picking tops/bottoms).
risk_geometry: Initial stop: 1/16 below setup low, capped at 5% of price; account risk ~2%. Scale-out at 1R to breakeven; trailing stop = lowest low of prior 2 bars; time stop ~7 bars; windfall rule on parabolic moves; drawdown table motivates caps (50% loss needs 100% gain to recover).
quote: as soon as your profits (a) are equal to or greater than your initial risk (b), you should lock in half of your profits and move your protective stop on your remaining shares to breakeven (c) (near your original entry).
chapter_anchor: Chapter 2, Landry's Rules and Money Management (pp. 11-16); Chapter 15-16 position management (pp. 191-206); Chapter 1 Drawdown (pp. 7-9)
notes: Direct inputs for RiskGate (5% initial-stop cap, ~2% account risk, one-direction discipline, never average down) and lifecycle (scale-out at 1R -> breakeven stop, 2-bar-low trailing, ~7-bar time stop). For 24/7 perps all these clocks must be bar-counted, not calendar-dated, to preserve V8 determinism; the drawdown-recovery asymmetry justifies the heat/cap discipline.

strategy_name: Preserve mode: stop migration Kijun->Tenkan and break-even protection
setup_summary: Exit-management ladder for trend trades: (1) initial stop = Kijun Sen minus buffer; (2) when open profit >= threshold (book: 300 pips FX) enter 'Preserve mode' and migrate stop to the Tenkan Sen to tighten it ('we do not want to give back all our profits'); (3) 'free trade' when the stop is at/above entry (breakeven) - profit guaranteed even on stop-out. Book notes Preserve mode is a conservative choice that foregoes some tail profit by design (captures ~30-50% of max profit); the day-trade plan adds 'once 12 pips profit reached, change stop to break even' and 'once 20 pips reached use Tenkan as stop'.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger = open profit >= preserve threshold while TS trending with position. Invalidation = TS is flat/higher than Kijun (keep Kijun as stop) or price retraces to stop. Also: if price is >200 pips from a FLAT Tenkan, exit (book's 'pip rule for flat conditions' - only fires when TS flat, not when trending).
risk_geometry: Stop: Kijun - buffer -> Tenkan - buffer after preserve threshold -> break-even. No target; expiry none. All distances volatility-scaled in crypto.
quote: Preserve mode is where we move our stop from the Kijun Sen to the Tenkan Sen to tighten our current stop. We do not want to give back all our profits... With this conservative strategy, we are going to get stopped out for a profit or get stopped out for a minimum loss when we are wrong.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 3 backtest, Preserve mode (p.63, pp.83-88); day-trade stop ladder in Chapter 8 (pp.185-187)
notes: This is a lifecycle rule (stops vs dead-thesis are separate exits in V8): a deterministic stop-migration ladder driven by realized profit in R/ATR units. The 'free trade' state is an explicit break-even lifecycle state. The flat-vs-trending qualifier on the 200-pip exit is a good dead-thesis discriminator.

strategy_name: Portfolio risk framework: allocation cap, mandatory stop, R/R<1 target
setup_summary: Book's trading-plan risk layer: never allocate more than 20% of funds to one position; a stop order is mandatory on every entry ('people lose all their money because they forget or did not want to place a stop order'); never risk 100% of portfolio at once because of gap risk; keep system-level risk/reward < 1.0 (avg winner > avg risk); cap max entry risk (daily FX: 250-300 pips, including buffer, per trade); risk per month = drawdown budget; no add-ons for the base plan; weekly re-placement of alerts.

risk_geometry: Position size bounded by 20% allocation and per-trade risk cap; stop always present; targets structure-based.
quote: we always use a stop and never risk 100 percent of our portfolio at one time (money management)
chapter_anchor: Chapter 2 'Components of a Trading System' (pp.41-44); Chapter 3 (p.73); Chapter 4 'Post-Analysis' (pp.137-147)

strategy_name: Day-trade session circuit breakers (max losses/trades per day)

strategy_name: Cost-structure constraint on short-horizon strategies (spread/fee dominance)

strategy_name: Protective stop-loss order
setup_summary: Glossary definition: a stop-loss order automatically liquidates an open position at a specific price to minimize exposure if the market moves against the position (e.g., long USD at 156.27 with a stop at 155.49). Falsifiable: every open position carries a resting protective stop at a defined price level.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: position opened. Invalidation: no protective stop present, or stop not executable by venue.
risk_geometry: Entry at market/limit; protective stop at a specific price (e.g., 78 pips below entry in the glossary example); stop is an automatic liquidation, distinct from a discretionary exit.
quote: Stop Loss Order Order type whereby an open position is automatically liquidated at a specific price. Often used to minimize exposure to losses if the market moves against an investor's position.
chapter_anchor: Glossary entry 'Stop Loss Order'
notes: Directly reinforces V8 risk_geometry stops and the simulator STOP_FIRST semantics; perp venues support resting stops natively.

strategy_name: Fundamental-announcement whiplash risk
setup_summary: Chapter 10 (pp.161-174) covers fundamental announcements; the index shows the book distinguishes 'Trading Days Versus Trending Days' (p.167), warns of 'Increased Risk with Trading Fundamental Announcements' (pp.167-169), and references 'Whiplashes' (p.169) and 'Not All Fundamental Announcements Move the Market' (p.183). Falsifiable: price around high-impact scheduled announcements is subject to two-sided whipsaw that raises stop-out probability versus normal sessions.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: a high-impact scheduled announcement window. Invalidation: if a given announcement class shows no elevated volatility/whipsaw in the local venue data, the rule does not apply.
risk_geometry: Risk-reduction rule rather than entry rule: reduced size, wider stops, or no new entries during event windows; 'trading fundamental announcements' carries increased risk (p.167-169).

strategy_name: OCO bracket exits
setup_summary: The index shows the book covers One-Cancels-Other (OCO) orders (pp.27, 43): a bracket where two resting orders (typically take-profit and stop-loss) are attached to a position and the filling of one cancels the other. Falsifiable: an OCO pair guarantees a single terminating exit at either the target or the stop.
trigger_invalidation: N/A - order-management structure; requires both resting orders valid simultaneously.
risk_geometry: Bracket exit: target above (long) and protective stop below attached at entry; first fill cancels the counterpart order; glossary 'Stop Loss Order' provides the protective leg.

strategy_name: Sovereign short on banking-system size vs fiscal capacity
mechanism: When an economy's banking/aggregate obligations dwarf its capacity to service them (government revenues), credit is mispriced as risk-free; historically such ratio extremes precede default, and repricing arrives as a confidence-driven step-change, not a gradual decay.
setup_summary: Compute the ratio of a system's banking-sector obligations (or total debt) to its government revenues; when the ratio exceeds historical danger thresholds (Ireland >25x annual tax revenue; Spain and France >10x), short the credit. Bass validated the heuristic against Reinhart-Rogoff's sovereign-default history before positioning. Transferable perp-application: an aggregate-leverage regime filter — when venue-wide OI or system leverage reaches extreme multiples of spot cashflow/volume, tail-deleveraging risk is underpriced.
trigger_invalidation: Thesis invalid if the entity actually runs sustained primary surpluses (Bass: 'the only way things can work out... If they start running real budget surpluses') or if confidence never reprices despite the ratios.
risk_geometry: Bet sizing is probability-weighted (11bps premium paid on Greek default insurance vs ~70% expected loss); no stop specified; counterparty rule — trade only with firms least likely to fail and demand daily collateral posting.
quote: The first thing we tried to figure out was how big these banking systems were, especially in relation to government revenues. We took about four months to gather the data. No one had it. ... Historically, such levels of government indebtedness had led to government default.
chapter_anchor: Preface, 'The Biggest Short' (~14/396)
notes: Not directly tradeable in BTC perps (no sovereign credit market); kept as a regime-filter/methodology transfer: the ratio heuristic (obligations vs capacity to service) is a falsifiable tail-risk indicator that could gate V8 risk or the simulator regime.

strategy_name: Paper exposure vs deliverable supply (futures OI vs physical / perp OI vs spot depth)
mechanism: When open interest in a derivatives contract far exceeds deliverable/spot supply, a crisis can seize up the paper market and decouple it from the underlying; holders of 'paper' exposure own a claim, not the asset — settlement and venue choice are part of the position.
setup_summary: Bass's venue rule: hold physical gold, not gold futures, because outstanding futures contracts exceeded available gold and the futures market was likely to seize up in a crisis ('people who thought they owned gold would find they owned pieces of paper instead'). V8 analog: when perp open interest is a large multiple of spot depth/volume, the perp can dislocate from spot under liquidation cascades — funding and basis blow out, insurance-fund risk materializes; the simulator cost model should represent perp-spot decoupling in high OI-to-depth regimes rather than assuming clean convergence to spot.
trigger_invalidation: Venue/risk rule, not a directional thesis; no invalidation beyond the OI-to-deliverable ratio regime itself.
risk_geometry: Hedging/venue selection: prefer the settlement-robust exposure; monitor OI-to-spot-depth as a regime gate on the cost model and on perp-vs-spot basis assumptions.
quote: You need physical gold. ... when the next crisis struck, the gold futures market was likely to seize up, as there were more outstanding futures contracts than available gold. People who thought they owned gold would find they owned pieces of paper instead.
chapter_anchor: Preface, 'The Biggest Short' (~21/396)
notes: The 'more contracts than gold' phenomenon is structurally identical to perp OI exceeding liquid spot depth. Feeds the simulator's basis/funding dislocation model and a risk rule on venue exposure; it is a cost/settlement lesson, not a signal, hence direction NONE.
book: Boomerang - Travels in the New Third World 2012

strategy_name: Terminal Price Bar (T-bar) initial-test reaction validation
mechanism: the initial bar that tests the entire PRZ defines the reference for validity; a valid reversal must react to the zone on/near that bar, and the T-bar extreme sets the invalidation level
setup_summary: After a pattern completes in the PRZ, identify the T-bar = the first bar whose range tests the full set of harmonic numbers. Valid reversal: price stabilizes on the T-bar (bullish) or the T-bar closes below the harmonic range (bearish), then continues in the reversal direction. Violation of the T-bar extreme = dead reversal thesis (and, per Ch 12, the trigger level for the failed-pattern continuation trade).
trigger_invalidation: No reaction on the initial test, consolidation then resumption of the prior trend ('a common sign of a failed setup'), or close beyond the T-bar extreme/PRZ - each invalidates the reversal.
risk_geometry: T-bar extreme is a frozen reference used both for the reversal stop and for the continuation entry 1-2 bars beyond it (see failed-pattern finding); no other exit geometry stated.
quote: In an ideal reversal, the price bar that tests all of the numbers in the PRZ is called the Terminal Price Bar (T-bar).
chapter_anchor: Ch 10 'Price Action in the Potential Reversal Zone (PRZ)', pp. 185-190; Ch 12 p. 234
notes: Operationalizes as a still_valid-style lifecycle condition for any zone-reversal family: 'close stays on the reversal side of the T-bar extreme'. Falsifiable and cheap to compute from 1h bars.

strategy_name: 2% risk cap + minimum 2:1 R:R + three-step position sizing
setup_summary: Pre-trade risk protocol: (1) maximum dollar risk on any trade = 2% of account equity, computed before the session; (2) per-share/per-contract risk = stop distance from the strategy (technical level, not arbitrary); (3) max position = max_risk / risk_per_share. Do not take any trade with reward:risk below 2:1 (a logical stop that would risk >2% of equity means skip the trade).
trigger_invalidation: Trigger = setup with R:R >= 2:1 and stop inside the 2% cap. Invalidation = stop placement requires >2% equity risk or R:R < 2:1 — pass on the trade regardless of attractiveness.
risk_geometry: Position = (2% x equity) / (entry - stop); min reward:risk 2:1; stop always at a reasonable technical level (VWAP, MA, level), never tightened below the technical level to force a ratio.
quote: The absolute maximum traders may risk on any trade is 2% of their account equity.
chapter_anchor: Ch 3 (Risk and Account Management; Three-Step Risk Management), lines 345-424
notes: Corroborates V8 RiskGate design: 2% fixed-fractional cap, R-multiple targets, stop-at-technical-level admission, skip-trade-on-over-risk. Book adds the breakeven math: with a 2:1 R:R gate a trader can be wrong 40% of the time and still profit — a rationale V8 can encode as a minimum-R:R admission check. Directly transferable to perp sizing (notional/leverage-adjusted).
book: How to Day Trade for a Living - Tools, Tactics, Money Management, Discipline and Trading Psychology 3rd edition

strategy_name: Never average down a losing position; scale into winners only
setup_summary: If the thesis level is lost (e.g., support breaks), exit — do not add to the losing position to lower average cost; averaging down wins ~85% of the time but the ~15% of trades that fail blow up the account, and the one bad trade can end the career. Scaling is permitted ONLY into winners (add on validated continuation, e.g., re-adding shorts after a failed retest of a broken level).
trigger_invalidation: Trigger = thesis invalidation (level/MA/VWAP break). Invalidation: any add-on-a-losing-position is prohibited; re-entry is allowed only when the setup re-forms (e.g., price returns below the broken level).
risk_geometry: Honor stop at the technical level; position added only on favorable confirmation; LABU and Amaranth/Brian Hunter case studies are the cautionary evidence (margin call / forced liquidation).
quote: Averaging down does not work for day traders... 85% of the time you will profit when you average down. But the 15% of the time you are wrong, you will blow up your account.
chapter_anchor: Ch 7 (Trade Management and Position Sizing), lines 1103-1157
notes: Maps to V8 lifecycle/risk rules: ONE exposure per direction, dead-thesis exit (stops vs still_valid), no re-entry until setup re-forms. Especially load-bearing in perps where leverage turns 'averaging down' into a liquidation event (margin-call dynamic = funding + leverage amplification). Note the author reports a distribution asymmetry (85/15) that is the classic martingale ruin argument — falsifiable only as a risk-behavior rule, not as an edge claim.
book: How to Day Trade for a Living - Tools, Tactics, Money Management, Discipline and Trading Psychology 3rd edition

strategy_name: Session time-of-day regime + daily giveback bracket
setup_summary: Session segmentation with strategy-to-session mapping: Open (first ~1.5h, highest volume/volatility) is the most profitable period — trade momentum/VWAP with full size; Mid-day (low liquidity) is the most dangerous — cut size, tighten stops, only reversal/VWAP/MA/S-R setups, never momentum; Close (last hour) is directional — trade with the institutional flow. Hard daily bracket: stop trading (or move to simulator) after giving back 30% of Open-session profits during Mid-day/Close.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger = session regime transition (liquidity expansion/contraction). Invalidation = daily giveback bracket exceeded (loss of 30% of Open profits) — trading stops for the day.
risk_geometry: Position size tiered by session (largest at Open, smallest mid-day); stops tight mid-day; the 30% giveback bracket acts as a daily P&L stop independent of per-trade stops.
quote: I am not allowed to lose more than 30% of what I have made in the Open during Mid-day and the Close.
chapter_anchor: Ch 7 (Trading Based on the Time of Day), lines 1599-1615
notes: Crypto is 24/7 with no 9:30 bell, but session structure exists (UTC daily boundary, Asia/Europe/US liquidity, funding-settlement windows at 00:00/08:00/16:00 UTC). Maps to the time feature group (session regime) plus a daily-equity giveback bracket in lifecycle — a deterministic daily stop on realized session P&L that is fully implementable in the replay clock model (no wall clock needed).

strategy_name: 1-3% risk-per-trade sizing with risk-free scaling
mechanism: risk control dominates the trading equation because wins/losses/order are unpredictable; sizing by stop distance and a small % of capital keeps drawdowns survivable
setup_summary: Risk 1-3% of trading capital per trade (novices 1%); position size = (capital x risk%) / stop distance, rounded down; never risk more than ~10% of the instrument price as a stop (about 5% is reasonable); never widen a stop; always place a stop (Rule #1/#2). After taking a first profit equal to the amount risked, move the stop to breakeven (risk-free trade) and scale out remaining units at further Fib targets. Recompute sizing when the account shrinks/grows; cap concurrent open positions.
trigger_invalidation: N/A - a position-sizing and stop policy, not an entry setup.
risk_geometry: Position sizing formula: shares/contracts = risk_dollars / stop_distance. E.g., $100k account x 3% = $3000 / $2.00 stop = 1500 shares. Stop never exceeds ~10% of instrument price. First target = risk amount, then breakeven stop, then trailing to .618/.786 levels.
quote: We suggest using a risk in the range of 1 percent to 3 percent of total trading capital on any one trade.
chapter_anchor: Ch 11, Money Management
notes: Directly maps to V8 RiskGate (deterministic admission, heat cap, one exposure per instrument/direction, position sizing by stop distance). Critically relevant to perps where margin-based sizing at 10-50x leverage ignores true risk. 'Risk-free trade' (breakeven after first target = risk) is a lifecycle-rule candidate.
book: Trade What You See - How To Profit from Pattern Recognition 2007

strategy_name: Per-trade equity risk cap (equity management formula)
mechanism: quantifying worst-case loss per trade before entry and capping it as a fraction of equity preserves staying power, so a sub-50% win rate can still be profitable
setup_summary: Never risk more than 5% of trading equity on any single trade (0.5-2% for professional money managers); typical protective stops are 30-50 pips; require risk:reward at least 1:1 and habitually 1:1.5 ($500 risk -> $750 planned gain); the book demonstrates that a 30% win / 70% loss record with $300 losses and $2,000 wins still nets a profit.
trigger_invalidation: Rule violation (not a trade thesis): a trade that cannot meet the RR floor or per-trade risk cap must be declined regardless of setup quality ('if the trade does not meet the equity management requirements, you need to have the discipline to pass on the trade').
risk_geometry: Sizing: risk per trade = stop distance x position size; stop distance 30-50 pips typical; risk cap <=5% of equity (0.5-2% pros); RR floor 1:1, habit 1:1.5; book's loss-endurance table: 1 loss survivable at 50% risk vs 19 losses at 5% risk.
quote: The rule of survival at trading is to never risk more than 5 percent of your equity on any given trade.
chapter_anchor: Ch 12 'The Equity Management Formula' and 'Risk versus Reward' (pp.192-197)
notes: Direct input to V8 RiskGate: per-trade risk cap, RR minimum, and the loss-endurance table. Crypto's high leverage makes the cap more binding (a 1% adverse move is ~3x the book's 30-pip stop on typical FX majors). Note the book's formula is expressed on margin, which for perps should be equity-normalized.
book: The 10 Essentials of Forex Trading - The Rules for Turning Trading Patterns Into Profit 2007

strategy_name: Pre-submitted protective stop at entry (no mental stops)
mechanism: mental stop-loss orders fail under drawdown because hope and fear override discipline; a pre-submitted protective stop placed at the same instant as the trade is the only reliable loss boundary
setup_summary: Every entry must be accompanied by a protective stop placed at the moment of entry — a little beyond the last major support (longs) or last major resistance (shorts) — managed as an OCO pair with the profit limit so a fill on one cancels the other; never rely on mental stops and never move the stop after entry.
trigger_invalidation: Rule violation: trading without a pre-submitted stop is treated as exposure to financial self-destruction; moving a stop after entry is prohibited ('do not move it if you are trading an OCO order').
risk_geometry: Stop: pre-submitted at entry, beyond last major support/resistance (book's narrative re-entry example: '10 pips below the low of the morning star'); every buy order carries a sell limit (profit) + sell stop (loss), and vice versa; OCO cancellation so no working order is left exposed.
quote: protecting yourself as you trade is called placing a protective stop-loss order in the market at the same time as you execute the trade.
chapter_anchor: Ch 12 'What Is Equity Management?' (pp.188-192); Ch 2 'Types of Orders' (p.27)
notes: Maps to V8's lifecycle invariant: stops are frozen refs set at candidate creation, never moved — matching 'do not move it'. 24/7 crypto makes unmonitored mental stops especially fatal (no session close to save a runaway position; leverage can liquidate in hours).
book: The 10 Essentials of Forex Trading - The Rules for Turning Trading Patterns Into Profit 2007

strategy_name: Cost drag arithmetic: net return equals gross return minus all-in costs, compounded
mechanism: Every fee, spread, slippage and financing point taken from each trade compounds against gross edge over time, so a strategy only has net edge if gross per-trade expectancy exceeds the all-in cost hurdle, and the hurdle grows with turnover (costs ~= 1% per 100% annual turnover).
setup_summary: For any strategy, compute net per-trade expectancy = gross expectancy - all-in cost rate (taker/maker fees + spread + slippage + funding + financing). A strategy is net-negative regardless of win rate if gross expectancy per trade does not clear the all-in cost per trade; the 2.5pp/yr cost gap consumed ~70% of the potential market accumulation over 50 years (Exhibits 4.1-4.2). Falsifiable: simulated net return must equal gross minus modeled all-in costs on every trade.
trigger_invalidation: If gross per-trade expectancy does not exceed all-in cost per trade, the strategy is net-negative regardless of win rate; if turnover rises without edge rising proportionally, net edge decays. 'We get precisely what we don't pay for.'
risk_geometry: Cost layer, not entry/stop: book's equity baseline ~0.5% per side round-trip (turnover cost rule), plus expense ratio, sales charges, taxes; in perp terms funding (8h), taker/maker fee, spread, slippage per holding period; no stated stop/target.
quote: Gross market return, minus costs, equals net return for investors as a group.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 4 (The Relentless Rules of Humble Arithmetic), Chapter 17 (reprise, QED 3)
notes: Direct input to V8 simulator cost model. Perps add a 24/7 funding stream absent from equities and leverage multiplies notional cost; the 'tyranny of compounding costs' argument is the strongest, most falsifiable claim in the book.
book: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing - The Only Way to Guarantee Your Fair Share of Stock Market Returns 2007

strategy_name: Hyperactivity drag: returns decrease as motion increases
mechanism: Overtrading burns edge: the most active traders pay costs on every round trip and their net returns lag the market by the cost of their motion; the empirical reference is the most-active 1/5 of traders turning portfolios >21%/month and netting 11.4% vs the 17.9% market return in 1990-96.
setup_summary: Bin any strategy's trades by frequency; if net expectancy per unit of turnover is not positive, reducing trade frequency raises net return. Buffett's maxim: 'For investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases.' The book's prescription for clients: 'Don't do something. Just stand there.' Falsifiable on perp data by bucketing accounts/holders by turnover and measuring net PnL after all costs.
trigger_invalidation: If per-trade net expectancy is positive, frequency per se is not the problem; the penalty exists only where turnover costs exceed the edge added by the extra trades.
risk_geometry: No entry/stop; a portfolio-level trade-frequency/turnover cap, plus full cost charging in the simulator for every extra trade; aligns with V8's buy-and-hold-style low-turnover baseline.
quote: For investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 1 (A Parable, Buffett's fourth law), Introduction (active-trader study, 1990-96)
notes: 24/7 low-friction markets and instant leverage maximize the temptation to overtrade; a per-instrument frequency cap in the risk/lifecycle layer directly encodes this finding.
book: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing - The Only Way to Guarantee Your Fair Share of Stock Market Returns 2007

strategy_name: Data-mined paradigms decay: backtested strategies are promoted only after they worked and edges get arbitraged away
mechanism: Paradigm decay: any factor or weighting scheme promoted as a new paradigm (fundamental indexing, value/small tilts, January effect, Nifty Fifty, new-economy funds) was marketed only after its best days; past backtested margins (~1-2%/yr) are eroded by costs and by investors bidding away the claimed systematic mispricing.
setup_summary: A backtested strategy is introduced only after it has already outperformed; the promoters never explain why the factor is structurally underpriced. Test the persistence claim: if the strategy was right in the past because of a transitory mispricing, investor demand prices it away ('if these paradigms actually have been right in the past, won't they therefore be wrong in the future?'). For V8: a PROPOSED expert whose edge rests on backtest alone is suspect until it clears frozen OOS, because selection-on-past-winners is the promotion mechanism itself.
trigger_invalidation: An edge with a stated structural cause for persistence (a real, unrepaired market friction) can persist; without such a mechanism the backtest is data mining.
risk_geometry: No trade geometry; a governance rule: no promotion on in-sample/backtest results; registry experiments must beat the simple baseline on frozen OOS (aligns with V8 constitution rules 6/14/15).
quote: No one would have the temerity to promote a new strategy that has lagged in the past. ... if these promoters of the purported new paradigms actually have been right in the past, won't they therefore be wrong in the future?
chapter_anchor: Chapter 14 (Index Funds That Promise to Beat the Market)
notes: Crypto factor decay is fast; this is the book's argument for why V8's evidence-bound falsification program exists. 'There have been many new paradigms over the years. None has persisted.'
book: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing - The Only Way to Guarantee Your Fair Share of Stock Market Returns 2007

strategy_name: Mr. Market discipline: quotations are for convenience - react to thesis, not price noise
mechanism: Short-term prices are a voting machine (emotions), long-term a weighing machine (fundamentals); the investor who reacts to every quote converts a winner's game into a loser's game by trading on emotion instead of on thesis validity - 'market quotations are there for his convenience, either to be taken advantage of or to be ignored.'
setup_summary: Separate the expectations market (short-term price/emotion) from the real market (fundamental value); exit a position only when the underlying thesis is invalidated, not when the quote moves against it. In V8 terms this is exactly the separation between stop-loss (risk) and dead-thesis still_valid (thesis) exits, and the rule that the still_valid condition is computed from structure, not from noise.
trigger_invalidation: If a quote move reflects genuine thesis invalidation (fundamental change), ignoring it is wrong; the discipline is about not being driven by transitory emotion.
risk_geometry: Exit logic: risk stop and thesis still_valid are different exits; no noise-based triggers; the book adds that speculation's contribution washes out long-term, so noise exits are pure cost.
quote: In the short run the stock market is a voting machine . . . (but) in the long run it is a weighing machine.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 2 (Rational Exuberance, Graham quote), Chapter 16 (What Would Benjamin Graham Have Thought about Indexing?)
notes: 24/7 trading and leverage amplify the cost of noise-driven exits; this book independently motivates V8's existing still_valid vs stop separation as a lifecycle invariant.
book: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing - The Only Way to Guarantee Your Fair Share of Stock Market Returns 2007

strategy_name: The passive index is the null hypothesis every active strategy must beat net of all costs
mechanism: Zero-sum-after-costs arithmetic: the aggregate active investor must earn the market gross return minus all costs; a low-cost passive portfolio is the guaranteed baseline, so the probability an active manager beats the index decays with horizon (Monte Carlo: ~29% at 1yr, ~15% at 5yr, ~9% at 10yr, ~5% at 25yr, ~2% at 50yr given 0.25% vs 2% cost).
setup_summary: The index fund is 'guaranteed to win ... every year, and every month and week, even every minute of the day' because gross market return minus intermediation cost equals net investor return. For V8: every expert's results must be measured against a passive benchmark of the traded instrument, net of funding + fees + slippage, not just against 'edge > 0'; the low-turnover baseline is the null hypothesis.
trigger_invalidation: If the passive baseline itself is structurally weak in an instrument (e.g., holding a perp long pays funding), the bar is lower - but the baseline must still be computed and reported honestly.
risk_geometry: Benchmark construction: low-turnover, all-in-cost-inclusive, stated in the experiment protocol; measure every candidate stream against it.
quote: The index fund is guaranteed to win not only over time, but every year, and every month and week, even every minute of the day.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 3 (Cast Your Lot with Business), Chapter 12 (Profit from the Majesty of Simplicity, Exhibit 12.1)
notes: In perps there is no free passive index - a long perp pays funding and decays, so the benchmark must be constructed (e.g., spot-hold net of funding) and stated; this is the cost floor every V8 expert must clear.
book: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing - The Only Way to Guarantee Your Fair Share of Stock Market Returns 2007

strategy_name: Core Risk Management Discipline (RR, stops, break-even, scaling)
mechanism: Fixed risk controls (min 1:2 reward:risk, 2% per-trade risk cap, break-even at 1R, never add to losers, max-loss rules) convert a raw edge into positive expectancy by keeping losses small and letting winners run.
setup_summary: Rules: (1) minimum 1:2 risk:reward before entry; (2) risk <=2% of equity per trade; (3) move stop to breakeven once profit equals initial risk (1R); (4) never add to losing positions; (5) treat any add-on to a winner as an independent new trade with its own risk (per-lot stops); (6) maximum loss / drawdown cap; (7) stop placement methods: two-day low minus 10 pips, or 20 pips below support, or parabolic SAR trailing; (8) keep a trading journal as enforcement.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any new position. Invalidation: 1R stop, 2R target, or break-even relocation; the journal is the enforcement mechanism.
risk_geometry: Stop: two-day low minus 10 pips (or 20 pips below support); target at least 2R; breakeven at 1R; trailing via parabolic SAR or two-bar extreme; risk fraction 2%.
quote: the rule of moving your stop to break even as soon as your position has profited by the same amount that you initially risked
chapter_anchor: Ch. 7, 'Risk Management', p. 71-75
notes: Mostly already present in V8 RiskGate (risk_percent_sizing, break_even_stop, volatility-based stops, max_drawdown_cap). Confirms existing rules; the explicit 'never add to losers' and 'add-ons are independent trades' rules are candidate RiskGate refinements.

strategy_name: Fixed Fractional Money Management
mechanism: risking a fixed fraction of equity per trade keeps per-trade risk constant in capital terms so that losing streaks compound geometrically but never wipe the account
setup_summary: Position size is computed so the capital at risk on each trade equals a fixed percentage of account equity; the trading plan must state the maximum percentage of capital risked per trade and a reward-to-risk ratio target. This is an admission-time rule applied to every CandidateDraft regardless of direction.
trigger_invalidation: Invalid if the risked fraction scales with conviction or recent win rate (that is a different, adaptive sizing rule); the fraction must be a frozen registry constant.
risk_geometry: risk per trade = fixed % of equity; stop distance defines risk; notional derived from equity, risk %, and stop distance; reward-to-risk target set in plan
quote: reward-to-risk ratios, fixed fractional money management, and potential trailing stop-loss strategies. These all have to do with the proper placement of stop losses in relation to the larger goals of preserving capital, reducing risk...
chapter_anchor: Ch.6 Chapter Summary (p.216-217); plan element 'Maximum percentage of trading capital risked on each trade' at Ch.6 Plan the Trade (p.214); Index: Fixed fractional money management 200-201
notes: Corroborates V8's RiskGate admission and risk_geometry. Crypto perp leverage (up to 100x+) makes per-trade risk fraction the binding constraint; funding and taker fees slightly erode the fixed fraction if not modeled in cost.

strategy_name: Trailing Stop-Loss

strategy_name: Periodic Loss Limit (Stop Trading for the Period)
mechanism: a pre-committed periodic loss threshold halts all trading for the period at the point of monetary loss, forcing reassessment instead of revenge trading
setup_summary: The trading plan fixes daily, weekly, and monthly loss limits: at the point of monetary loss the trader stops trading for the given period, regardless of subsequent setups that appear.

mechanism: only strategies with demonstrated positive expectancy, verified by backtesting on past price data, are admissible to live use; money management presupposes a positive-expectancy strategy

strategy_name: Fixed-fractional risk and reward-to-risk ratio discipline
mechanism: Risk a fixed percentage of equity per trade by construction: stop distance and position size are chosen so max loss equals the percentage cap; a high reward-to-risk ratio (3:1 ideal, 2:1 practical) lets a trader be right less than half the time and still profit.
setup_summary: Per trade, cap risk at a fixed fraction of account equity (book example: 3% -> 30-pip max stop on a $1/pip mini-lot for a $1,000 account; recommends the cap as a flexible maximum, e.g. 'no single trade can have a stop loss that exceeds 4% of total equity', not a rigid per-trade %). Set profit targets to a multiple of the stop (2:1 practical, 3:1 ideal, 4:1 aggressive), adapting to market conditions; require positive expectancy overall and ~10x required margin as account capital.
trigger_invalidation: N/A — risk rule; invalidation is a capital-preservation constraint, not a market signal.
risk_geometry: Stop: distance chosen so that stop-magnitude x pip-value x size <= equity % cap. Target: 2-4x the stop distance. Position sizing: micro/mini/standard lots scaled to the cap; the book explicitly warns against setting stops at arbitrary pip values that ignore market conditions (e.g. 30-pip stop inappropriate for a weekly head-and-shoulders).
quote: a more adaptable rule might be to require that no single trade can have a stop loss that exceeds, for example, 4% of total equity.

strategy_name: 2% risk per trade, rule of three, and premium breakeven math
mechanism: fixed-fraction sizing bounds ruin while position sizing in multiples of three and premium-aware breakeven math keep one loss from erasing a winning streak
setup_summary: Never risk more than 2% of equity on any single trade; size positions in multiples of three (all-in three lots or legging one lot at a time, all-out/leg-out exits); compute the required win rate from the premium - a $95 premium needs 19 winners per loser, a 5:1 payoff needs >=1 win in 5, and >80% accuracy is required to profit buying $80 premiums. Book also flags time-of-week risk asymmetry: an $80 premium position Monday is riskier than the same on Thursday (more time for things to go wrong). V8 mapping: RiskGate max-risk-per-exposure as % equity + breakeven-aware evaluation of each expert's required win rate.

strategy_name: Deep-out-of-the-money (DOOM) weekly tail insurance
mechanism: cheap convexity on extreme ladders pays off disproportionately in the rare large moves, acting as portfolio insurance against selloff surprises
setup_summary: Hold one deep-out-of-the-money play ($10-20 premium, ~5-6:1 payoff) each week as an insurance policy for unexpected selloffs, mixed with high-probability legs (book mixes: 3 DITM + 1 DOOM, or thirds DITM/ATM/DOOM). DOOM pays when markets move big (book: 'black Monday' 2015, oil crash 2015 - DOOM and breakout plays catch the moves); it will not pay off most weeks, so expectancy must be evaluated over many weeks. Falsifiable: a constant DOOM-like tail basket on an index has positive net expectancy over periods containing >=1 tail event.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: none - continuous standing position. Invalidation: none per-trade; strategy-level risk is that it never pays while costs accumulate - book: 'it will not pay off all the time'.
risk_geometry: Entry: market on the extreme ladder (premium $10-20); risk = full premium; target = $100 payoff (5-6:1); expiry = end of period; book warns selling the extreme ladders (the reverse leg) is dangerous because 'markets that are extended become extended for a fundamental reason'.
quote: It's not a bad idea to put on one DOOM play each week as an insurance policy for when the unexpected occurs. The only caveat with such an approach is it will not pay off all the time.
notes: The $100/0 fixed-payoff structure does not exist on perps; the transferable lesson is portfolio-level: mixing low-probability high-payoff legs with high-probability legs, evaluated over many weeks, and the warning against fading extended markets. strategy_name: Fixed-fraction 3% risk per trade
mechanism: Capping each trade's dollar risk at a fixed fraction (3%) of equity makes per-trade outcome variance a constant fraction of the account regardless of instrument or stop distance; combined with a mandatory stop it bounds ruin.
setup_summary: Every strategy in the book sizes the position so the pip-distance to the stop risks 3% of account capital; returns are consistently quoted as 'X% return if we take a 3% risk' (e.g., a 15-pip risk at 1.5:1 R yields a '2% return'). The corollary rule is unconditional: 'Always put a stop loss for every trade' - the stopless ('naked') trade is named as the primary account-blowing behavior.
trigger_invalidation: Not a market-trigger rule but a sizing/admission constraint: violated if a trade is sized so its stop exceeds the 3%-of-equity budget, or if a position is entered without a stop.
risk_geometry: Entry/stop/target per strategy; this rule fixes size such that (entry - stop) distance x position size = 3% of equity.

strategy_name: Win-rate is not expectancy (asymmetric payoff trap)
mechanism: Cutting winners at a small fixed gain while holding losers until they recover produces a high win rate but negative expectancy, because loser size is unbounded while winner size is capped.
setup_summary: Falsifiable claim: any rule that (a) exits winners at a small fixed gain and (b) holds losers until they turn positive produces a win rate near 95% but a net loss, since average loss dwarfs average win. The author demonstrates this with a 20-trade demo (19 winners, 1 loss) that nets a loss. V8 implication: expert evaluation and registry (Screening) verdicts must be computed on expectancy / profit factor and payoff geometry, never on win rate.

risk_geometry: Anti-pattern as described: entry anywhere, take-profit very small (near 0R), stop effectively absent (hold to positive). The book states this geometry loses despite a 95% win rate.

strategy_name: Drawdown as the controlling performance metric (return-to-drawdown)
mechanism: A trader who risks a 50% drawdown to make 100% is closer to ruin than one who makes 20% with a 2% drawdown; institutional capital is allocated on largest drawdown, not headline return.
setup_summary: Decision rule: performance is judged first by worst drawdown ('What is your biggest drawdown?') and by return-to-drawdown ratio, not raw return. Author compares Trader A (100% gain / 50% max drawdown) with Trader B (20% gain / 2% max drawdown) and concludes B is superior and A is 'an accident waiting to happen.'

mechanism: Deliberate early acceptance of small losses is what prevents account-destroying losses; failure to take a strategic loss is the common genesis of major trading disasters.

strategy_name: Backtest overoptimization and hypothetical-returns skepticism
mechanism: Markets are nonstationary; any strategy can be curve-fit to history, so in-sample/hypothetical excellence is not evidence of future edge, and hypothetical results are routinely marketed as actual.
setup_summary: Methodology rule: 'the past does not equal the future'; overoptimized backtests are easy to construct in hindsight and are marketed deceptively (book cites a CFTC complaint for misrepresenting backtested returns). Trading plans must be validated out-of-sample, and hypothetical results must be explicitly distinguished from actual results.
trigger_invalidation: If an expert's advantage survives out-of-sample and forward simulated replication on frozen OOS, nonstationarity alone does not disqualify it; claims of edge without such evidence are inadmissible.
risk_geometry: None — methodology.

mechanism: Trading without stops while taking profits quickly defers all risk to a single catastrophic loss; in a leveraged 24/7 market the deferred loss becomes a margin call / liquidation.

strategy_name: Pattern-Height Measure Rule (target projection)
setup_summary: For any chart pattern, target = breakout price plus (up breakouts) or minus (down breakouts) the pattern's height (highest peak to lowest valley). Per-pattern hit rates: ascending triangle up-breakout 72%, ascending triangle down-breakout 58%, rectangle 55%, symmetrical triangle 46%, double top 44% (half-height works 73%), triple top 48%, H&S top 53%. For a closer target, multiply the height by the hit-rate fraction before applying it; discard targets that imply absurd moves or sub-zero prices.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: pattern confirms (close beyond boundary); compute target = breakout +/- height. Invalidation: if projected % move is unreasonably large (e.g., a 69% gain on an H&S bottom) or predicts a below-zero price, discard; cross-check the target against overhead resistance/support (HCRs, prior peaks/valleys, round numbers) — a target lining up with a support level is more credible.
risk_geometry: Target = breakout +/- height (optionally height x hit-rate); the book uses this to set sell/take-profit levels for both buy and sell setups and as a sanity check on whether to hold. No entry or stop; no expiry.
quote: Take the height of most chart patterns and add it to the breakout price for upward breakouts or subtract it from the breakout price for downward breakouts. The result is the target price.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 24 (Chart Pattern Sell Signals); Ch. 21 (Measuring Flags and Pennants)
notes: Directly informs V8 risk_geometry target_r: replaces the fixed 1.0R default with a structure-derived target and provides per-pattern calibration priors. The hit-rate-weighted adjustment is a deterministic, falsifiable refinement for the simulator.

strategy_name: Round-Number Support/Resistance and Stop Placement
setup_summary: Prices cluster at numbers ending in zero (20, 30, 40...; in crypto, e.g., 10k/50k/100k): traders place buy/sell orders, targets, and stops at round numbers, so these levels show support and resistance even where price has never traded. Use the next closest round number to guess where price will stall; exit just ahead of it (sell at 79.93 not 80); NEVER place orders or stops at round numbers because that is where everyone else is — clustered stops there create stop-running avalanches.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: price approaching a round number = expected stall/reversal zone; use for target selection and stop placement (place stops away from round levels). Invalidation: strong trend punches through the round number (SAR is probabilistic, not a hard barrier); measure rule/momentum then takes over.
risk_geometry: Used to set targets (sell just before the round number) and to place stops away from round numbers to avoid being gunned. No expiry.

strategy_name: Minor-Low Stop Placement and Trailing
setup_summary: Place stops a penny-to-dime below the nearest prior minor low rather than below the whole pattern bottom (pattern-bottom stops are often too far — average ascending-triangle height is 13%, median 11%, so a pattern-bottom stop implies ~13% average loss). Raise the stop to below the prior minor low whenever price closes at a new high. strategy_name: Non-ergodicity, data snooping and backtest validation

strategy_name: Fixed fractional sizing with fractional Kelly weighting, correlated-exposure cap, and drawdown time-outs
mechanism: risking a fixed small fraction of equity per trade makes every loss smaller than the last (Zeno-like asymptotic approach to ruin), and because loss sequences are asymmetrical (a wipeout ends the game, a win does not guarantee survival), survival depends on bet size, not edge

Contracts = allowed risk divided by risk-per-contract; never widen the stop to fit more contracts. Weight positions by fractional Kelly (half-Kelly F=(bp-q)/b from win rate and avg win/avg loss, only after >=30 trades). Portfolio rules: stand aside or trade smaller on an equity-curve downside break; take a time-out after 2% daily / 5% weekly / 10% monthly drawdown. Coin-flip demonstration: betting 10% of a $100 bankroll 1,000 flips wipes out with >90% probability; 1% bets drop wipeout below 5%.
trigger_invalidation: Risk of ruin is bounded by the fixed fraction; invalidation thresholds are the 2%/5%/10% daily/weekly/monthly drawdown limits that trigger a mandated pause (the 'penalty box').
risk_geometry: Position sizing (account-level), not entry geometry: stop distance unchanged while size = risk-fraction x equity / per-contract risk. Correlated exposure capped to one direction per correlated group.
