strategy_name: Protective stop on every position: sell stop below support (long), buy-to-cover stop above resistance (short)
mechanism: A pre-placed stop at the thesis-invalidating level caps loss per exposure; risk is not inherent to the position side but to failing to protect capital
setup_summary: Every long carries a sell stop below current price at the level where the trader would no longer hold; every short carries a buy-to-cover stop above current price. The book's stance: shorting is not inherently risky ('the bull walks up the stairway but the bear jumps out the window' - prices fall faster than they rise), and 'It is not the practice of shorting that is risky, but rather the actions of the trader who fails to protect his capital.'
trigger_invalidation: n/a (risk rule).
risk_geometry: Stop = structural level below support (long) / above resistance (short); the book gives no ATR-multiple rule, placement is at a level where the position thesis no longer holds.
quote: Just like with a long position, a protective stop order can be used to limit loss on a short position. A protective stop-loss order for a long position is called a sell stop.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 10 'Short Selling' (protective stops)
notes: Foundation for V8's RiskGate stop semantics; in perps, high leverage makes structural stops essential but wick-through-stop risk (liquidity sweeps) is acute, so stop placement must anticipate sweep-and-reclaim rather than sit exactly at the level.
book: Getting Started in Candlestick Charting 2008

strategy_name: Reward:risk >=2:1, stop at failure point with max-distance cap, 2% account risk per trade
mechanism: Protecting capital is paramount: define reward and risk before entry; a stop placed at the technical failure point (not arbitrary) with a max-distance cap, and per-trade risk capped as a fraction of equity, keeps single-trade losses survivable.
setup_summary: Before any entry compute reward:risk = (target - entry) / (entry - stop): require at least 2:1 (ideally 3:1). Place the initial stop at the setup's failure point (pattern low/high or broken level), not to exceed 10% (swing) / 15% (long-term) of price from entry; cap loss per single trade at 2% of total equity; diversify (book model: max ~20% of account per position).
trigger_invalidation: Not a signal — applies to all entries. A ratio of 1 is a poor ratio; if the required stop distance exceeds the cap (e.g., ~10% on a volatile name), skip the trade or shift to a lower timeframe.
risk_geometry: Entry near confirmation close; stop at the technical failure point capped at 10%/15% distance; target at structure (S/R) or an R-multiple such that reward:risk >= 2:1; the 2%-of-equity per-trade risk drives position size (inverse of stop distance).
quote: I suggest always trying to select trade setups that will net at least twice as much potential gain as loss. And ideally, that ratio will be 3:1 or better on many trades.
chapter_anchor: Ch 10, Reward versus Risk, pp.207-209; Ch 8, Smart Investor Tip (2% account rule), p.161
notes: Maps to V8 risk_geometry (entry/target_r/stop_r) and RiskGate admission: add a minimum reward:risk gate and a stop-distance cap. The book's percentage caps are stock-world; for perps convert to ATR multiples given volatility. The 2%-of-equity per-trade rule aligns with the existing heat cap / position sizing logic.
book: Getting Started in Candlestick Charting 2008

strategy_name: Threshold-gated strategy evaluation
setup_summary: Do not react to short-run strategy P&L below a significance threshold: performance reports are reviewed only at pre-committed gates (a predetermined P&L/significance threshold), and small-sample outcomes are treated as noise. Taleb calibrates: a $100k gain implies ~2% probability the strategy is genuinely profitable, a $1M gain ~99%.
trigger_invalidation: If threshold-gated review selects different expert versions than continuous review on the same frozen OOS and the gate-selected versions fail to replicate out-of-sample, gating is mis-specified.
risk_geometry: Evaluation protocol, not a trade; no entry/stop/target.
quote: denying myself access to my performance report unless it hits a predetermined threshold
chapter_anchor: Ch. 12 (p. 180); calibration example Ch. 12 (p. 180)
notes: Direct design input for the lab/registry screening stage: expert versions are promoted/rejected only at significance-gated evaluation points, never on noisy short-run P&L. Fits V8's frozen-OOS + registry gating.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Path-independent position revaluation
setup_summary: For any open exposure, periodically re-run the entry decision as if flat: if the current MarketState would not generate the same CandidateDraft today, the position is dead regardless of entry P&L ('married to your position'). Soros example: short when market rallied to record highs, then 'covered and went very long' without embarrassment.
trigger_invalidation: Thesis invalidated when a flat-state re-run would not re-enter; the frozen still_valid check (dead-thesis) is a weaker special case of this rule.
risk_geometry: Exit on thesis-death via fresh-state re-evaluation rather than on P&L target; complements existing still_valid exits in lifecycle.
quote: If you owned no painting, would you still acquire it at the current price? If you would not, then you are said to be married to your position.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 13 'Path Dependence of Beliefs' (p. 187)
notes: Proposed as a lifecycle_rule addition: a periodic flat-state re-entry test layered on top of frozen still_valid logic. No dependence on venue microstructure; fully compatible with deterministic replay.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Negative-skew / blow-up risk cap
setup_summary: RiskGate must cap or reject any strategy whose payoff profile is negative-skew harvest (small frequent gains, rare catastrophic losses), sizing so the modeled worst-case tail (e.g., a deleveraging cascade) never exceeds the per-instrument heat cap. LTCM failed by assigning zero probability to the model itself being wrong.
trigger_invalidation: Cap is binding when a strategy's loss distribution shows realized tails beyond the modeled 99th percentile on frozen OOS, or when a negative-skew harvest strategy is not admitted through RiskGate without a tail-exposure cap.
risk_geometry: Risk rule: tail-exposure cap per instrument, one exposure per (instrument, direction), heat cap; not an entry setup.
quote: They made absolutely no allowance in the LTCM episode for the possibility of their not understanding markets and their methods being wrong.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 13 'Computing Instead of Thinking' (p. 189)
notes: Case-study storytelling (LTCM), not a controlled test, hence NARRATIVE. In crypto perps leverage and liquidation cascades make negative-skew harvest strategies acutely dangerous; the crypto analogue mechanism is the deleveraging_cascade / carry_unwind family.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: News-causality noise rejection
setup_summary: Treat every news-headline explanation of a price move as noise unless the move exceeded its usual magnitude; never use journalistic causal attribution as a feature. Sub-significance moves (< usual daily move, e.g., 1.03 Dow points at 11,000) have no adducible cause, and single-cause attribution is invalid in a multivariate world without isolating factors and reaching a >=90% confidence level.
trigger_invalidation: Methodology/design lesson: confirmed in V8 by the tape pipeline already excluding news text and wall-clock commentary from the decision path.
risk_geometry: None.
quote: the journalist claims to provide an explanation for something that amounts to perfect noise
chapter_anchor: Ch. 11 'The Bloomberg Explanations' (p. 165); multivariate/causality requirement p. 166
notes: Validates V8's determinism rule (no news feed, no wall clock in replay). 24/7 crypto commentary volume makes this guard more salient, not less.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Index-vs-component maximum bias
setup_summary: When aggregating across instruments, the maximum of an average is less volatile than the average maximum: components do not peak together, so component drawdowns run far deeper than the index drawdown. Cross-instrument max-based features (e.g., each perp's distance from its own high) must not be read as index-level signal.
trigger_invalidation: Statistical fact; applies whenever V8 features aggregate multiple instruments (currently single-instrument BTCUSDT).
risk_geometry: None.
quote: By a law of probability called distribution of the maximum of random variables, the maximum of an average is necessarily less volatile than the average maximum.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 11 opening (p. 163)
notes: A mathematical property of maxima, hence falsifiable. Becomes actionable when V8 expands to cross_market feature groups or altcoin perps: index-level stats understate component tails.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Conditional probability updating
setup_summary: Probability estimates must be conditional on the state actually reached: unconditional life expectancy at birth differs from conditional life expectancy given survival to age X. Applied to evaluation, a strategy that has survived N episodes has conditional properties different from its unconditional backtest properties; 'our operation has 1% mortality, so the 100th patient dies' is the fallacy to avoid.
trigger_invalidation: Estimation rule: any registry/replication estimate must condition on the sample-selection state (survival to that sample size), else it embeds the unconditional/conditional confusion.
risk_geometry: None.
quote: What these journalists confuse is the unconditional and conditional life expectancy.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 11 opening (p. 164)
notes: Basic probability logic (conditional vs unconditional), falsifiable. Guards the lab: replication estimates for a surviving expert version are conditional estimates and must be labeled as such, not pooled with unconditional statistics.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Kelly optimal leverage as upper bound (half-Kelly sizing)
setup_summary: Optimal leverage f = m/s^2 (Gaussian Kelly) maximizes compounded growth but estimation error in m and s means over-estimating leverage leads to ruin; therefore deploy at most half-Kelly and treat Kelly as an upper bound, never the operating leverage. Non-Gaussian reality is better handled by optimizing expected log-growth on Monte-Carlo returns matched to the first four moments (Pearson system) or directly on backtest returns.
trigger_invalidation: Sizing rule only; falsifiable at portfolio level: an active risk rule that size exceeds 1/|worst observed bar return| must be rejected as ruin-in-sample.
risk_geometry: Position size = leverage f on equity, capped at half-Kelly; hard ruin bound f < 1 / |max_negative_bar_return| (book's worked example: f=30.2 ruins on a -3.31% bar).
quote: The consequence of using an overestimated mean or an underestimated variance is dire: Either case will lead to an overestimated optimal leverage, and if this overestimated leverage is high enough, it will eventually lead to ruin: equity going to zero.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Optimal Leverage, pp.171-177 (Kelly, Monte Carlo, historical growth)
notes: Directly relevant to perp crypto where leverage is a free choice up to 100x+. Informative for V8's heat cap and position sizing: adds a Kelly-derived upper bound and the ruin bound f < 1/|worst return|. Note the constant-leverage corollary (see separate finding) is a contagion anti-pattern V8 should avoid.
book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

strategy_name: Constant Proportion Portfolio Insurance (CPPI)
setup_summary: To both cap maximum drawdown at -D and keep near-optimal growth: put only a fraction D of total equity in a trading subaccount and apply Kelly leverage f to it, keeping the rest in cash. Losses never draw cash from the subaccount (so size shrinks toward zero as drawdown grows), and at a new equity high-water mark the subaccount is reset to D of total equity. Doubling down on the drawdown-limit property: reducing leverage to cap drawdown is highly nonlinear (cutting f by ~7x was needed to halve simulated max DD from 0.999 to ~0.5).
trigger_invalidation: Risk/lifecycle rule; falsifiable at portfolio level: with the scheme, realized account drawdown must never exceed -D on any backtested path, and order size must be monotonically decreasing in drawdown.
risk_geometry: Size = f * D * equity; no stop loss needed; reset to D-of-equity at new high watermark; account wind-down when subaccount is exhausted.
quote: We can simply set aside D of our initial total account equity for trading, and apply a leverage of f to this subaccount... We can then be assured that we won't... suffer a drawdown of more than -D in our total account... this scheme serves as a graceful, principled way to wind down a losing strategy.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Constant Proportion Portfolio Insurance, pp.179-182
notes: A clean, deterministic drawdown-cap scheme that fits V8's gate architecture (no wall-clock, no learned component). Book notes CPPI is per-strategy (not for multistrategy accounts where winners subsidize losers) and cannot protect against overnight gaps/suspended markets - in 24/7 crypto the gap risk is lower but flash-crash wick risk remains (see flash_crash finding).
book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

strategy_name: Stop-loss placement is regime/strategy-class contingent
setup_summary: For mean-reversion strategies a stop loss always lowers backtested Sharpe because of survivorship bias - the successful catalog excludes the mean-reverting series that regime-changed into trending - yet it prevents ruin when that regime change happens; so place the stop beyond the backtest maximum intraday drawdown so it never triggers in-sample but catches the black swan. For momentum strategies a continuously updated momentum signal is a de facto stop (loss means momentum reversed, so exit or reverse); stops are therefore a natural, low-cost component of momentum experts and remove the tail risk that mean-reversion experts carry.
trigger_invalidation: Falsifiable: on an MR family, a stop placed inside the backtest max intraday drawdown must lower in-sample Sharpe; a stop placed beyond it must leave in-sample performance unchanged but truncate the worst OOS tail.
risk_geometry: MR stops: beyond backtest max intraday drawdown (wide, rarely hit); momentum stops: signal reversal / time-based exits, no separate hard stop required.
quote: It is more accurate to say that stop loss always lowers the performance of mean-reverting strategies when the prices remain mean reverting, but it certainly improves the performance of those strategies when the prices suffer a regime change and start to trend!... we should impose a stop loss that is greater than the backtest maximum intraday drawdown.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Stop Loss, pp.182-184
notes: Distinguishes dead-thesis exits from stop exits in a way that maps onto V8's still_valid mechanism: for trend/momentum experts the still_valid signal is the stop (a la trend_pullback's uptrend-persists check); for future mean-reversion experts the stop must sit beyond the in-sample max drawdown. Also flags that a stop is only as good as continuous liquidity - relevant to crypto wick-throughs.
book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

strategy_name: Leading risk indicators as regime filters (VIX/TED/order flow)
setup_summary: Leading risk indicators (VIX, TED spread, HYG, MXN, ONN/OFF, and sudden large negative order flow on risky assets) can gate trading in the next period, but they are strategy-specific: VIX>35 was good for the buy-on-gap stock strategy (Sharpe 1.5->1.4, return 8.7%->17.2%) yet catastrophic for the FSTX opening-gap strategy (return 13%->2.6%, Sharpe 1.4->0.16). The filter must therefore be validated per strategy, and backtesting rare crises invites data-snooping.
trigger_invalidation: Falsifiable per strategy: the indicator's high state must shift the conditional forward return distribution of that strategy (measured OOS). Invalidation: no shift, or the shift flips sign OOS.
risk_geometry: Regime gate only: skip entries (or reduce size) while the indicator is in its risky state; no position-level geometry.
quote: If the preceding day's VIX is over 35, then the day's annualized average return drops to 2.6 percent and the Sharpe ratio to 0.16. Clearly, VIX tells us to avoid trading on the following day.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Risk Indicators, pp.184-186
notes: For perp crypto the VIX/TED analogs are less clean; candidate leading indicators are funding-rate extremes, basis, and perp aggregate open-interest/leverage - these are observable 24/7 (no VIX open-to-close regime). Lesson for V8: a regime filter is strategy-specific, so it belongs per expert (registry-gated), and backtests over rare crises are data-snoop-prone.
book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

strategy_name: Kelly capital allocation under a binding leverage cap concentrates
setup_summary: With multiple strategies and a broker/account gross-leverage cap Fmax much smaller than the sum of individual Kelly leverages, proportionally scaling all positions down (the naive fix) is suboptimal; the worked two-strategy example shows concentrating all buying power into the strategy with the highest independent growth rate (F2=Fmax) beats the proportional scaling (growth 0.96 vs 0.82). Applicable whenever a portfolio-level leverage constraint binds.
trigger_invalidation: Portfolio-level: given two uncorrelated strategies and a binding gross leverage cap, concentrating in the highest-growth one yields higher compounded growth than proportional scaling (book's Example 8.2).
risk_geometry: No position geometry; allocation rule over strategies, relevant only when a portfolio leverage/heat constraint binds.
quote: The upshot of that example is that when Fmax is much smaller than sum|Fi|, it is often optimal (with respect to maximizing the growth rate) to just invest most or all our buying power into the portfolio or strategy with the highest mean excess return.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Example 8.2, pp.173-175
notes: V8 has no ranker/router (absent by default, gated), so this is a recorded methodology lesson for any future allocation layer rather than an implementable component; it also cautions against a naive 'scale everything down' heat-cap implementation once multiple experts are active.
book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

strategy_name: Stop-loss protection is contingent on continuous liquidity
setup_summary: A stop loss only guarantees a maximum loss if a market is open with liquidity present: in the May 6 2010 flash crash, market makers withdrew to stub quotes ($0.01) and a stop on Accenture executed at $0.01. Stops also cannot protect across overnight gaps or suspended markets. Implication: execution models and risk gates must assume stop fills degrade in liquidity-withdrawal states rather than always filling near the stop price.
trigger_invalidation: Falsifiable in simulation: modeled stop slippage under a low-liquidity/high-volatility state must be materially worse than the normal-state fill price; a simulator that always fills stops at their limit price overstates protection.
risk_geometry: Stop fills: gap-through/slippage modeling in stressed states; no protection assumed across market suspension.
quote: In some extreme circumstances, stop loss is useless even if the market is open but when all liquidity providers decide to withdraw their liquidity simultaneously. This happened during the flash crash of May 6, 2010... an unfortunate sell stop order on Accenture... was executed at $0.01 per share that day.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Stop Loss, p.183 (flash crash, Arnuk & Saluzzi 2012)
notes: Crypto perp has no traditional gaps (24/7) so stop-loss gap risk is reduced, but liquidity can still vanish in deleveraging cascades and liquidation-engine wicks can trade through stop levels by large multiples; V8's canonical simulator (STOP_FIRST, fill-at-close, gap semantics) should model stop slippage under stress states rather than assuming limit fills.
book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

strategy_name: Constant-leverage rebalancing 'selling into losses' is a contagion amplifier
setup_summary: Optimal-leverage schemes require keeping leverage constant: after a loss you must sell into the loss and after a gain buy more. When many funds hold similar positions and all follow constant-leverage risk management, one fund's forced liquidation forces others to liquidate - cited as a cause of the August 2007 quant meltdown (Khandani & Lo 2007). Sizing/rebalancing rules that mechanically de-leverage into drawdowns shared across the market amplify the drawdown they are meant to cap.
trigger_invalidation: Macro-level, not directly testable on one expert; the falsifiable version is that forced leverage-rebalance selling co-moves with other funds' liquidations during stress.
risk_geometry: None at position level; design caution for the sizing/heat-cap rule.
quote: This is because often many funds are holding similar positions in their portfolios. If one fund suffers losses... it is prone to liquidate positions across all its portfolios due to the constant leverage requirement, causing losses for all other funds that hold those positions... a vicious cycle.
chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Example 8.1: The Implications of the Constant Leverage Requirement, pp.170-171
notes: Directly relevant to crypto liquidation cascades (funding + leverage concentration). Design inference for V8: do not implement forced constant-leverage rebalancing that sells into losses; a heat cap or CPPI-style monotonically-shrinking size is safer than re-leveraging on the way down.
book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

strategy_name: Hypothesis-first, falsifiable, OOS-tested strategy research
setup_summary: Strategy development is a scientific loop: form a hypothesis about a specific market inefficiency, express it as a simple quantitative model, test against new unseen data, and when it underperforms seek a fundamental cause (e.g., the GLD/GDX pair stopped cointegrating until crude-oil was added) rather than piling on arbitrary rules. Simple linear models exploit an understood inefficiency; regime shifts and non-stationarity are why live-vs-backtest divergence happens, and the manager's role is high-level validity judgment while algorithms beat experts at rule execution (Kahneman).
trigger_invalidation: Process standard, not a strategy: a research action is invalid if it adds rules/indicators without a stated falsifiable mechanism and an OOS test.
risk_geometry: None.
quote: In science, we form a hypothesis, express it as a quantitative model, and then test it against new, unseen data to see if the model is predictive... Instead of blindly adding more rules, more indicators... we should look for a fundamental reason and then quantitatively test whether this fundamental reason is valid.
chapter_anchor: Conclusion, pp.187-189
notes: This is the book's core epistemology and matches V8's falsification mandate (evidence labels, frozen OOS, challenger-vs-registry evolution). Reinforces V8 rules: mechanism-first family design, no arbitrary rule accretion, registry-gated evolution, and evidence-bound claims.
book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

strategy_name: Unplanned averaging down (blowup trait)
mechanism: Adding to a losing position on dips without a pre-planned conditional rule and without a stop converts a temporary dip into ruin when the dip does not reverse
setup_summary: Anti-pattern: buy every 'line in the sand' as price falls, relying on a 'value'/narrative thesis while price keeps declining, with no predetermined stop and no plan for the event of continued decline. Carlos added Russian bonds at $52, $43, $30s, $20s — then sub-$10 — converting cumulative +$80M into a single -$300M quarter. The trait that made dip-buyers the 1992-1998 winners was the same trait that killed them in 1998.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any add-to-loser must be a pre-registered conditional rule with its own risk budget. Invalid: discretionary averaging-down with no plan; price breaks the registered add-condition or the pre-registered stop.
risk_geometry: Entry: bar close or limit after dips; stop: none (that is the failure mode); target: none; expiry: none — the anti-pattern is the absence of any pre-planned geometry.
quote: Both bought more bonds after the market declined sharply, but not in response to a predetermined plan.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 5, A Review of Market Fools of Randomness Constants (p. 79-80)
notes: Correlates with V8 position_scaling concept but inverts it: scaling into losers is admissible only as a registered conditional rule (one multiplicity unit with its own geometry), never as discretionary 'value' buying. On perps, averaging down without a stop compounds toward liquidation.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Expectation (probability x payoff), not hit rate, decides the trade
mechanism: The check is expectation = probability x payoff; frequency/probability alone is irrelevant without the magnitude of the outcome
setup_summary: Methodology: evaluate any strategy by expectation over its outcome distribution, never by win rate or directional accuracy. The book's worked example: 70% chance of +1% and 30% chance of -10% is net -2.3 — 'bullish' yet correctly shorted. A 90%-losing option position can still be the better side if the winning 10% pays 50x.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any expert evaluation. Invalid: strategy shows positive hit-rate but negative expectation, or expectation turns negative on honest out-of-sample distribution estimation.
risk_geometry: n/a — evaluation methodology.
quote: it is not how likely an event is to happen that matters, it is how much is made when it happens that should be the consideration.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 6, Bull and Bear Zoology (p. 88)
notes: 'Bullish or bearish are terms used by people who do not engage in practicing uncertainty.' For V8: expert scoring must be expectation-based over the simulated outcome distribution (simulator STOP_FIRST, cost model), not accuracy-based; mirrors the 'you are paid in dollars, not probabilities' point.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Observation-frequency effect: at short scales you see variance, not returns
mechanism: The noise:signal ratio explodes as the observation scale shrinks (1796:1 at one second for a 15%/10% process), so high-frequency monitoring misreads variance as signal
setup_summary: Methodology: a 15% return / 10% volatility process has a 93% probability of profit over a year but only 50.02% over a second; over one hour there are ~30 parts noise per part performance, over one second ~1796. Judge strategies on longer-window aggregates and never treat short-window P&L as evidence; the same strategy evaluated monthly vs daily is the same strategy with different emotional load.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any evaluation of an expert. Invalid: conclusions flip when the same strategy is evaluated on a longer observation scale; short-window P&L treated as signal.
risk_geometry: n/a — evaluation methodology; book notes the negative pang is up to 2.5x the positive one, so emotional reaction to short-window noise is systematically costly.
quote: Over a short time increment, one observes the variability of the portfolio, not the returns.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 3, Philostratus in Monte Carlo (p. 58), Table 3.1
notes: Crypto is 24/7, so the temptation to observe continuously is maximal; the lesson supports V8's bar-level determinism (no wall clock in replay), its event/available/ingested clock discipline, and longer-window registry evaluation instead of reacting to short-window equity moves.
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Cross-sectional problem: recent winners are best-fit to the latest cycle
mechanism: At any point the most profitable operators are those best fit to the most recent cycle, not the most skilled; ergodicity reverts them over a longer sample path
setup_summary: Methodology: dip-buying was the trait most desirable from 1992 to summer 1998 in emerging/high-yield markets; the dip-buyers dominated and displaced arguably better traders, then blew up together in 1998 when the regime flipped. 'The richest traders are often the worst traders' at any cross-section. For V8: an expert's recent top performance is regime-conditional, so registry promotion must be evidence-bound across regime samples, not extrapolated from the latest winners.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any registry promotion decision. Invalid: recent top performance reverses across regime samples; no regime-conditional evaluation was run.
risk_geometry: n/a — evaluation/registry methodology.
quote: at a given time in the market, the most profitable traders are likely to be those that are best fit to the latest cycle.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 5, Carlos the Emerging Markets Wizard (p. 74)
notes: Supports a regime_filter methodology component: crypto alternates sharply between trending and ranging regimes; a strategy's pedigree (e.g., 'this worked in the last 2 years') must be discounted for regime fit. Ties to ergodicity: 'The lucky fool... over the longer run he would slowly converge to the state of a less-lucky idiot.'
book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

strategy_name: Open-trade-equity heat cap (20% of core equity)
mechanism: the portfolio's deepest drawdowns arrive right after the biggest open-profit run-ups, so exposure must be capped when open profits run hot
setup_summary: Measure open-trade profits / core equity (cash + closed equity). When the ratio reaches 20%, stop taking any new positions until open equity subsides below the cap. Alternative lever: tighten the ATR stops or take partial profits.
trigger_invalidation: New admissions resume only when the ratio drops below the cap.
risk_geometry: Portfolio-level admission gate layered on per-trade stops; author states his biggest drawdowns follow his largest open-trade-profit periods.
quote: I cap my total open trade equity versus my core equity at 20 percent of my core equity.
chapter_anchor: Ch.5 'Overall Risk on the Portfolio'
notes: Maps to V8's RiskGate heat cap concept; on high-leverage perp accounts with uncapped exposure this is a real blowup guard, and open profits in crypto perps can spike intraday due to leverage.
book: The Trend Following Bible - How Professional Traders Compound Wealth and Manage Risk 2012

strategy_name: Overlapping risk layers: position count, per-contract dollar risk, margin-to-equity
mechanism: redundant overlapping risk caps catch concentration that any single measure misses
setup_summary: Admission requires ALL gates to pass: no more than 10 long and 10 short positions simultaneously; futures dollar risk per contract capped at $2,000-2,500 regardless of account size (so 1% of a large account cannot blow up one contract); margin-to-equity kept under 15% (author's comfort level).
trigger_invalidation: N/A — multi-layer admission gates; a trade is passed if any single gate fails.
risk_geometry: Portfolio-level caps layered on per-trade stop distance; the per-contract dollar cap was added after the author's mistake of risking $5,000/contract on a $500k account.
quote: I will not trade more than 10 markets on the long side and no more than 10 markets on the short side.
chapter_anchor: Ch.5 'Additional Risk Measures When Commodity Trading and Forex Trading'; Ch.6 Steps 4-5
notes: The per-contract dollar cap is a direct guard for perp position sizing at high leverage; margin-to-equity maps to a leverage cap. Position-count caps are largely moot for a single-instrument system but inform any multi-instrument expansion.
book: The Trend Following Bible - How Professional Traders Compound Wealth and Manage Risk 2012

strategy_name: Risk-of-ruin geometry ('100 bites of the apple')
mechanism: risk per trade determines how many consecutive losers are survivable; risk above ~1-2% materially raises the probability of ruin over a large trade sample
setup_summary: Assume worst-case streaks (author has personally seen 8-10 consecutive losers and drawdown durations exceeding 24 months; one 2011 loss exceeded the target due to a gap/limit move). Size so ~10 consecutive losers cannot materially dent equity: ~1% risk per trade. Supporting formula given: R = e^(-2a/d), where a = mean return, d = std dev.
trigger_invalidation: N/A — an expectation doctrine; 'your greatest drawdown is always ahead of you' is stated as invariant.
risk_geometry: Account-level doctrine governing per-trade risk %; the 'apple bites' mapping is 100 bites at 1%, 50 at 2%, ~33 at 3%, 20 at 5%, 10 at 10%.
quote: If you are risking 1 percent of your account on a trade, you get to have 100 bites out of the apple.

notes: The single most transferable risk lesson for high-leverage perp crypto: book explicitly warns risk >2% 'increases dramatically' ruin probability, and that drawdowns of 24-30 months are normal for the strategy — a V8 lifecycle/drawdown expectation note. strategy_name: Percent-of-equity risk sizing with position scaling by stop distance
setup_summary: Size each position so the maximum loss is a fixed percent of core equity (1.25% on the Global Diversified model, 0.75% on the Diversified model, with per-contract dollar caps of $2,000/$2,500). A tighter stop (or lower volatility instrument) permits more contracts 'for the same risk as a one-lot'; the journal repeatedly attributes enhanced returns to trading two-to-four contracts at identical percent risk. Falsifiable: contract count = floor((fixed_pct * core_equity) / stop_distance_in_dollars).
trigger_invalidation: No entry trigger; sizing rule applied at every admission. Fixed-dollar-per-contract cap (and 1.25% nominal risk) can still be exceeded by gaps/limit moves -- accepted, not preventable.
risk_geometry: Sizing from core equity (excludes open-trade equity); per-trade risk cap 0.75-1.25%; per-contract dollar risk cap; position scaling is a direct consequence of stop distance, not of conviction.
quote: What enhanced my return was that for the same risk I was able to put on two contracts. This underscores the power of position sizing.

strategy_name: Sector correlation cap (5% per sector, correlation filter within sector)
setup_summary: Cap portfolio exposure at 5% per sector; within a sector, take a new trade only if it does not push the sector's correlation past the threshold (e.g., a 10-year bond long was the last interest-rate trade because the 5% correlation quota was filled; corn+wheat longs were skipped once filled). Falsifiable: no new admission if sector aggregated exposure would exceed 5% of equity, or if pairwise correlation with an open position exceeds a fixed limit.
trigger_invalidation: No entry trigger; an admission is blocked when the sector/correlation quota is full regardless of signal quality -- 'no matter how good a trade looks, follow the plan.'
risk_geometry: Portfolio-level cap (5% per sector), not a per-trade stop; interacts with the heat cap; affects admission, not exit.
quote: I do not want to have more than 5 percent of my portfolio in any one sector. If I allocated heavier in a sector my correlations to risk would increase dramatically.

strategy_name: Take every signal; sequential statistical independence
setup_summary: Trade every signal, never skip, and never stop trading a market after a loss streak: the journal documents 9 losses in a row (Dec 2010-Jan 2011), 18 losses in a row (late 2011), and 6-7 loss runs, all taken mechanically; 'the prior trade has absolutely nothing to do with the next trade.' Cherry-picking or quitting a market after losses is described as a guaranteed path to the losing majority. Falsifiable: signal-to-admission rate = 100% with zero discretion.
trigger_invalidation: None -- this is a consistency constraint, not a market trigger.

quote: The prior trade has absolutely nothing to do with the next trade. One must take every trade via one's plan.

strategy_name: Gap/limit-move stop slippage is accepted, un-preventable risk
setup_summary: Even with stops placed immediately on entry, realized losses can exceed the planned per-trade risk because of gaps and limit moves (documented: a cotton long lost 1.5% instead of the planned 1.25% on an adverse gap; Swiss franc fell ~800 points in a day). The book's stance: this is irreducible uncertainty; the only complete prevention is not trading. Falsifiable: stop fills can be modeled with a slippage/overshoot term beyond the nominal stop level.
trigger_invalidation: None -- risk acceptance statement.
risk_geometry: Stop orders placed immediately on entry; nominal risk cap 0.75-1.25% can be exceeded by gap/limit events; no mitigation offered beyond accepting and not trading during unrunnable conditions.

strategy_name: Data/contract-spec integrity and model synchronization
setup_summary: A natural-gas data/contract mismatch (mini vs full contract) made the system miss a trailing-stop exit signal by 'a tick or so'; the author stayed short, later discovered the position was still open, and skipped a large continuation profit out of prudence. Lesson stated as 'always to get in sync with the model.' Falsifiable: every signal must be computed on the exact same instrument/contract and timestamps the model assumes; a data mismatch must be detectable, not silently actable.
trigger_invalidation: None -- integrity constraint.

strategy_name: Scale out in thirds with break-even stop (pay yourself as the market makes money available)
mechanism: Harvesting a partial position early converts the remainder into a risk-free state, cutting per-trade loss variance and guaranteeing net profit on tail exposure
setup_summary: Trade a minimum of 3 (or 4) size units. Take the first third off as soon as the market moves a small predefined amount in your favor (author: 4 tics in T-bonds, 1.5-2 full points in S&P). Take the second third at a longer-timeframe support/resistance or a test of a prior significant high/low, and simultaneously move the stop to the original entry (the 'risk-free opportunity'). Leave the last third running with a liquidate order just below a long's / just above a short's likely stopping point on a longer timeframe; do not chase the last tic.
trigger_invalidation: Trade is dead at the (initially predefined, later break-even) stop. Last third's thesis dies when price trades beyond the longer-TF stopping point (significant high/low).
risk_geometry: Initial stop predefined (author: ~6 tics on T-bonds); first take at small favorable move; second take at structure with stop moved to break-even; final trailing liquidate just beyond longer-TF significant high/low; author self-reports only ~1 in 10 trades was an immediate loser and 25-30% of losers first moved 3-4 tics favorable.
quote: I always, without reservation or hesitation, take off a portion of a winning position whenever the market gives me a little to take.
chapter_anchor: Ch11 / Taking Profits (scale-out regime)
notes: The 'risk-free opportunity' state is the mechanism V8 should formalize in ExposureBook/lifecycle: partial take-profit at small favorable move + stop-to-break-even converts remaining exposure to positive expectancy regardless of outcome. For perp crypto, scaling out also reduces funding-cost drag on open notional. This is position management, not an entry expert.

strategy_name: Minimum 3:1 reward-to-risk ratio per trade
mechanism: With reward:risk >= 3:1, breakeven win rate falls to 25%, so a win rate below 50% still yields positive expectancy - profitability decouples from prediction accuracy
setup_summary: Require target distance >= 3x stop distance on every trade (risk $1 for every $3 of profit potential). Combined with the scale-out regime, a winning-trade percentage below 50% can still be consistently profitable.
trigger_invalidation: Rule-level constraint; no thesis. Breakeven win rate for reward:risk R is 1/(1+R).
risk_geometry: target_r/stop_r >= 3.0. Note: V8's existing experts use target_r 1.0, so this is parameter guidance to screen, not a law.
quote: Ideally, your risk-to-reward ratio should be at least 3:1, which means you are only risking one dollar for every three dollars of profit potential. If your edge and the way you scale out of your trades give you a 3:1 risk-to-reward ratio, your winning trade percentage can be less than 50 percent and you will still make money consistently.
chapter_anchor: Ch11 / Taking Profits (risk-to-reward)
notes: The arithmetic is verifiable (breakeven WR = 1/(1+RR)); the book evidences no edge with 3:1 skew. For V8: raising target_r from 1.0 trades hit-rate for expectancy - worth an OOS screening variant, not an a priori change.

strategy_name: Market-structure-determined stop, not arbitrary dollar or risk-comfort amount
mechanism: The optimum stop is the level at which the probability the trade will not work is so diminished that closing is better; market structure locates that level better than an arbitrary dollar amount
setup_summary: Define each trade's stop from market structure (the level beyond which the setup thesis fails), never from an arbitrary dollar amount or from risk-comfort. If the dollar risk is uncomfortable, reduce position size; change a risk parameter only when technical analysis warrants it, never to satisfy comfort.
trigger_invalidation: The stop IS the invalidation. Moving the stop (e.g., closer to entry out of fear) is itself classified as an error.
risk_geometry: Stop at the structural point beyond entry-side support/resistance; for pullback entries the distance is small ('usually very little risk'); risk per trade known exactly before entry.
quote: Let the market structure determine where this optimum point is, rather than using an arbitrary dollar amount that you are willing to risk on a trade.
chapter_anchor: Ch11 / Stop-Loss Exit
notes: Consistent with V8's structural/ATR stops and frozen risk_geometry (the book lists moving a stop closer to entry as an error). In perp crypto, structural stops at swing points are known stop-run targets for liquidation cascades, so a pure swing stop is huntable - MEDIUM rather than HIGH; needs a stop-hunt-aware placement or ATR buffer.

strategy_name: Evaluate edges on sample sizes of 20+ trades, never trade-by-trade
mechanism: Per-trade outcomes are random relative to each other; only a committed series reveals the edge's true parameters and their decay
setup_summary: Judge success or failure over a minimum sample of 20 occurrences of the edge, not the last trade. The sample must be large enough to fairly test the variables and small enough that a decay in effectiveness is detectable before an inordinate amount is lost.
trigger_invalidation: Methodology-level; no per-trade thesis. A single edge occurrence is never evidence of anything.
risk_geometry: Know the exact dollar risk per trade and the accumulated worst case (losing all 20) before starting the sample.
quote: Your sample size has to be large enough to give your variables a fair and adequate test, but at the same time small enough so that if their effectiveness diminishes, you can detect it before you lose an inordinate amount of money. I have found that a sample size of at least 20 trades fulfills both of these requirements.

notes: Directly supports V8's series/registry evaluation and frozen-OOS gating: an expert hypothesis is judged across a candidate-episode series, never per episode; small-sample screening before any registry promotion.

strategy_name: Casino regime: rigid precise variables, take every signal, no subjective filtering
mechanism: Consistent profit requires participating in every event where the odds favor you; picking and choosing trades reintroduces prediction and destroys the probability edge
setup_summary: Entry variables must be absolutely precise, requiring no subjective judgment: if the market aligns to the rigid variables you have a trade, otherwise not - no extraneous factors. Commit to trading the next 20 occurrences of the edge no matter what, and never change the variables mid-sample. This duplicates how a casino operates: fixed odds + participate in every event.
trigger_invalidation: Methodology-level; the commitment is to the full sample. Deviating from the rigid variables is itself the failure.
risk_geometry: The methodology must specify exactly how much is risked to find out if the trade works (the stop), computed in the same timeframe as entry.
quote: The rules are simple: Trade your system exactly as you have designed it. This means you have to commit yourself to trading at least the next 20 occurrences of your edge - not just the next trade or the next couple of trades, but all 20, no matter what.

strategy_name: Predefine and accept the exact risk of every trade before entry
mechanism: Risk acceptance requires knowing the exact dollar risk before entry; comfort is adjusted by position size, never by changing the technical risk parameter
setup_summary: Before any trade, know exactly the dollar cost of finding out whether the trade will work, and accept it (worst case: losing all 20 trades of the sample). If the dollar amount is uncomfortable, reduce position size (contracts/shares) or use simulated brokerage - never change the technical stop parameter to feel better.
trigger_invalidation: Rule-level; a trade taken without a predefined risk is by definition a violation.
risk_geometry: Predefined stop and $ risk per trade before entry; position sized so the accumulated 20-trade worst-case loss is bearable (author's example: S&P 3-point risk x 3 contracts = $2,250/trade, $45,000 for 20).
quote: My risk is always defined before I enter a trade.

strategy_name: Thinking in probabilities (five fundamental truths)
mechanism: Expecting a known outcome makes disconfirming market information threatening and triggers pain-avoidance errors; believing each edge's outcome is unique removes the threat and the error source
setup_summary: Operate from five beliefs: every moment in the market is unique; every edge has a unique outcome; you don't need to know what happens next to make money; potential for loss exists in every trade; outcomes are random relative to each other at the micro level and consistent only over a series. Neutral expectations prevent block/discount/distort/deny perception errors.
trigger_invalidation: Psychological framework, not a market thesis.
risk_geometry: None. The regime-level requirement is predefined risk + accepting any outcome.
quote: To think in probabilities, you have to believe that every moment in the market is unique, or more specifically, that every edge has a unique outcome.

strategy_name: Edge decay: no static variable set captures shifting market dynamics
mechanism: The set of active participants and their beliefs changes continuously, so the underlying dynamics of market movement change; any rigid snapshot of variables decays in effectiveness
setup_summary: A fixed set of market variables (a snapshot of a fluid system) may work well for an extended period, then its effectiveness diminishes as traders enter and leave with new ideas of high and low. Compensate by trading in bounded sample sizes that detect decay before an inordinate amount is lost, while keeping a consistent approach.
trigger_invalidation: Framework; decay is detected by comparing successive sample blocks, not by market signal.
risk_geometry: None.
quote: No snapshot (rigid set of variables) can take these subtle changes into consideration. You can compensate for these subtle changes in the underlying dynamics of market movement and still maintain a consistent approach by trading in sample sizes.

strategy_name: Predefine risk before entry
mechanism: unknown outcomes make risk quantification a mandatory precondition for entry; only consistent winners define risk in advance
setup_summary: Before any entry, the stop distance (invalidation price) and the money the trader is willing to spend to find out if the trade works are fixed in advance; entry happens only with this predefinition in place. Claim: traders who predefine risk before entry are the consistent winners, and 'not predefining your risk' is one of the three most common and costliest trading errors; a stop placed in the market is not the same as accepting the risk.
trigger_invalidation: Violated whenever a position is opened without a predefined stop/risk level; the rule is the requirement itself, not a price condition, so any stopless entry invalidates the episode.
risk_geometry: Entry: any, but only with a pre-set stop (price level where the edge is considered dead) and a defined max-loss 'spend to find out' amount decided before entry; loss framed as cost of doing business.
quote: only the consistent winners define their risk in advance of putting on a trade

strategy_name: Cut losses on thesis invalidation, not on P&L
mechanism: a standing stop alone is not acceptance; the exit must fire when the market invalidates the trade's premise, independent of current P&L
setup_summary: Exit without hesitation whenever the market shows the trade's premise is not working, regardless of entry P&L. Bob CTA anecdote: he placed a stop but bailed at entry when the market ticked against him, then watched the trade run 500 points — the book's point being that a stop in the market is not the same as accepting the risk. Claim: 'cut losses without reservation or hesitation when the market tells them the trade isn't working' is a defining trait of consistent winners.
trigger_invalidation: Thesis is dead when the invalidation condition fires; the error is holding past invalidation while hoping, which the book calls a passive-loser failure mode.
risk_geometry: Stop and dead-thesis are distinct exits: stop is risk geometry (max loss level), dead-thesis (still_valid) is the conditional premise failure; both must be executable without hesitation.

strategy_name: Take every edge signal (casino model)
mechanism: consistent results come from sample size over a fixed edge, never from picking which edges will win
setup_summary: Define an edge as a fixed behavior pattern with a higher probability of one direction; then take every trade that conforms to the edge and never skip or favor edges based on hunches about the next outcome. Two-layer belief: at the micro level each trade is random/statistically independent; at the macro level a large sample converges to the edge's expectancy (casino blackjack 4.5%-edge analogy).
trigger_invalidation: Falsifiable claim: for a fixed edge definition, wins/losses are randomly distributed (no serial dependence in the sequence) and realized outcome converges to expectancy as sample size grows — directly testable in the V8 lab.
risk_geometry: Per-trade risk still predefined (see NEW_predefined_risk); position size constant across edges; every trigger fires an entry.

setup_summary: Enter only when the edge's defining signal has actually manifested in the market, and take every manifestation; anticipating a signal that has not yet formed is evidence the trader is convinced he will miss out. The book lists getting in too early/too late, hesitating at signals, and moving stops closer to entry only to get stopped out as self-generated errors, not market-generated errors.

strategy_name: More analysis is not the path to consistency (black hole of analysis)

Claim: traders who react to losses by adding analytical tools get worse — the more they learn, the more they expect from the market and the more painful its failure to comply becomes, until consistency is lost.

setup_summary: All price movement is a function of what individual traders believe is high vs low; a constant unknown set of hidden variables (sidelined traders, position changes, exit intent) means no single trade's outcome is knowable regardless of pattern quality. Claim: 'it takes only one other trader, anywhere in the world, to negate the positive potential of your trade'; hence no setup is ever exempt from risk predefinition.

Claim: without a self-imposed end — stop, target, or expiry — a losing trade is a passive loser that can consume everything, and 'once you're in a losing trade, you don't have to do anything to keep on losing.'

strategy_name: Trailing stop for trend protection
mechanism: A stop that ratchets with the favorable extreme lets a winner run while capping giveback: position is closed only if price retraces the trailing distance from its best level
setup_summary: Exit rule: after entry, place a stop trailing N units (book: 100 PIPs) behind the favorable extreme; if USD/BRL falls to 1.84 then rises to 1.85, the position closes at 1.85; if it continues to 1.80 the stop ratchets to 1.81 - 'keep your position open as long as possible (maximizing gains) while continuing to protect yourself from any downside.' Combined with a protective buy-stop above resistance to cap losses (50 PIPs) if the counter-move never comes.
trigger_invalidation: Exit rule, not an entry: always active once in position; the trade-off is stop distance vs. false-exit frequency - tighter stops exit on noise (the book's USD/BRL example set the stop beyond the resistance level to 'give yourself some margin for error').

strategy_name: Four-tier unit limits: single market / closely correlated / loosely correlated / direction
setup_summary: Portfolio-level heat caps in units: max 4 units in a single market; max 6 units in one direction across closely correlated markets (e.g., crude + heating oil, gold + silver, the currencies as a group); max 10 units in one direction across loosely correlated markets (e.g., gold + copper); max 12 units total in one direction (long or short) across the whole book. Being 'loaded' = at the cap.
trigger_invalidation: N/A — portfolio risk limits.
risk_geometry: Binds aggregate risk across correlated exposures; per the book, even with caps a single gap day (Oct 1987 rate cut) lost 40-60% of equity on a concentrated short book.

strategy_name: Notional-account de-scaling: reduce trading size 20% per 10% drawdown
setup_summary: Trade against a notional account (size set yearly). Each time equity is down 10% from the original account size, reduce the notional by 20% (e.g., $1M down $100k -> trade as $800k; a further 10% off $800k -> $640k), until equity recovers to the yearly starting level. This shrinks position risk multiplicatively as drawdown deepens.
trigger_invalidation: N/A — equity-adaptive sizing rule.
risk_geometry: All position sizes scaled by the reduced notional until recovery; asymmetric (de-scales fast, rescales via yearly reset).
quote: The Turtles were instructed to decrease the size of the notional account by 20 percent each time we went down 10 percent of the original account.

strategy_name: Consistency and rule adherence as the alpha; concentration of yearly profits
setup_summary: A mechanical system covering every decision (markets, sizing, entries, stops, exits, tactics) is followed exactly, because yearly profits concentrate in two or three large trades, so any skipped signal can materially change the year. Turtles with the best records consistently applied the entry rules; those fired or with the worst records failed to enter consistently or changed rules subtly (e.g., slowing unit adds), which inverted the intended effect. Conviction must be built by personally backtesting on historical data, not by others' summaries, so the trader keeps executing through multi-month losing stretches.

risk_geometry: N/A.

If a signal was skipped or missed, this could have a great effect on the returns for the year... I always say that you could publish my trading rules in the newspaper and no one would follow them. strategy_name: Scale out of losers, scale into winners (add-on-strength)
setup_summary: Risk-management rule: scale out of losing trades and scale into positions that are in profit; Plan 3's behavior rule restates it as 'only add to profitable positions'. Claim: if the scaled position then declines, losses are smaller; if it continues rising, gains are larger.
trigger_invalidation: Adding to a winner that reverses against the add; the rule explicitly prohibits adding to losing positions.

strategy_name: Fixed per-trade risk cap with R-multiple target (1% stop / 2% target)
setup_summary: Size positions so a fixed stop distance implies a fixed dollar risk: 'if you don't want to lose more than $100 on a single trade and you seek a risk-to-reward ratio of 1% to 2%, then you shouldn't open a position greater than a $10,000 mini-lot.' Breakeven arithmetic: 1% stop / 2% target (1:2 R) is break-even at a 33% win rate; risking 2% instead of 5% per trade dampens the impact of loss streaks.
trigger_invalidation: Not applicable - a sizing identity; the 33%-win-rate-at-1:2-R:R breakeven is arithmetic, not an empirical claim.
risk_geometry: stop_distance = 1% (or risk_dollars / notional), target = 2% (2R); the book's rule-of-thumb is R:R = 1:2 with a fixed fraction of account risked per trade.

strategy_name: Fixed-distance trailing stop on the most recent extreme
setup_summary: A trailing stop sits at a fixed distance below the most recent high (30 PIPs in the example): as price rises the trail ratchets up, superseding the original stop, and executes when price retraces to the trail level (e.g. entry 1.3469, stop trails to 1.3499 after price reaches 1.3519).
trigger_invalidation: Breach of the trail level executes the stop (the intended exit); no other invalidation given.
risk_geometry: trail_distance fixed (30 PIPs example); example also has take-profit +50 / initial stop -20 PIPs; the trail supersedes the original stop once triggered.

strategy_name: Move stop to breakeven once the position is in profit
setup_summary: Behavior/risk rule from Plan 2: once a position's value is positive, move the stop-loss up to the entry price so the trade can no longer lose money (the cost is that the trade exits at breakeven on any retracement to entry).
trigger_invalidation: Retracement to entry stops the position at breakeven - the intended, bounded cost of the rule.
risk_geometry: stop moves from initial level to entry once position value >= 0; profit target unchanged.
quote: Move stops to breakeven when position value is positive

strategy_name: Consecutive-loss daily stop (circuit breaker)
setup_summary: For traders placing multiple trades per day: establish a mechanical rule that after 3 consecutive losing trades you quit for the day. The book generalizes this into contingency plans for 'a string of losses or a large decline in your account balance' and pairs it with 'avoid seeking revenge after losing trades.'
trigger_invalidation: Mechanical rule: reset on the next day (in 24/7 perp replay, a rolling 24h window).
risk_geometry: 3 consecutive losing trades -> no new entries for the rest of the period; paired with a no-revenge-trading rule.
quote: after 3 consecutive losing trades, you quit for the day.

Worked example: a 100-PIP loss on the same position is 20-25% of capital on 20-25:1 accounts but 2% on a 2:1 account.

strategy_name: Reduce/close exposure before scheduled high-volatility news events
setup_summary: Volatility spikes around planned news releases; if you cannot afford the loss a release might trigger, close the position or scale back leverage beforehand. The book also shows how to quantify baseline noise from realized volatility (USD/CAD weekly mean ~100 PIPs, max ~135) so event spikes are distinguished from routine fluctuation.
trigger_invalidation: Event passes without the feared spike (opportunity cost); the rule is a pre-event exposure decision, not a directional call.
risk_geometry: Pre-event action: close position or scale back leverage; no stop geometry given by the book.
quote: volatility may spike around certain planned news releases. If you think that a big move is likely and you can't afford the loss that the news might trigger, close your position or scale back your leverage.

strategy_name: Overtrading discipline (fewer, longer, higher-conviction trades)
setup_summary: After excessive leverage, 'the biggest strategic mistake committed by novice traders is overtrading' - scalping without preparation, too many simultaneous positions. Remedy is quantitative: 'Instead of trying to earn 50 PIPs twice a day, aim for 200 PIPs once a week,' hold positions longer, and 'there is no rule that says you need to be in the market at all times' - sit out when the market is gyrating or the strategy gives no signal.
trigger_invalidation: Not applicable - behavioral discipline; the book's attribution example (30 trades in 3 weeks for +253 PIPs) argues fewer trades would have matched the result.
risk_geometry: Raise per-trade profit threshold and hold duration; lower trade count; optional per-day trade cap.
quote: Instead of trying to earn 50 PIPs twice a day, aim for 200 PIPs once a week.

strategy_name: Change of Polarity (old support becomes new resistance)
mechanism: trapped_position_gravity - traders who bought near old support (or were stopped out there) are emotionally attached to their entry price; rallies back to that level trigger their break-even exits, converting old support into supply and old resistance into demand.
setup_summary: After a tested support breaks, the first rally back into the old support zone should stall and reverse (SHORT); after tested resistance is cleared, pullbacks to the old resistance zone should hold (LONG). The level should be tested a few times before applying the principle, and it works as a zone, not an exact price.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: price re-enters the flipped zone after the break. Invalidation: a close back through the zone in the breakout direction (old support re-conquered on a close) voids the flip thesis.
risk_geometry: Entry on the reaction into the flipped zone, ideally with a confirming candle (e.g., hammer confirming polarity support; bearish engulfing at polarity resistance); stop beyond the flipped zone; target toward the next structure; old support zone can be a band (e.g., $116-$117.50) rather than one line.
quote: Old support becomes new resistance and old resistance becomes support. This is what I call the 'change of polarity' principle... The most important price on any chart is the price at which you entered the market.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 11, Candles with Trend Lines - The Change of Polarity Principle, pp. 205-211
notes: The psychological mechanism (break-even exits by trapped longs) transfers directly to crypto, where prior range extremes, round numbers and liquidation clusters are heavily traded. Natural frozen-ref design: ref = previously tested support/resistance level. This also supplies the 'why' behind V8's failed_breakout still_valid rule (close stays below the old level).

strategy_name: Cluster of Candles / Convergence of Signals at One Price
mechanism: signal_convergence - several independent candle and Western signals stacking at the same price area (support or resistance) magnify the significance of that area, because each signal is an independent estimate of the same supply/demand boundary.
setup_summary: At a support/resistance area, count the independent candle signals (engulfing patterns, hammers, doji, piercing patterns, shooting stars, windows) and Western signals (trend lines, MAs, retracements, change of polarity) landing at the same price: the more that converge, the higher the probability the area holds. Location matters more than signal shape - a buy pattern completed at a resistance area is not a buying opportunity.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: >=2 independent signals at the same ref. Invalidation: a close through the convergence zone voids the cluster; a signal formed at the wrong location (buy signal at resistance, sell signal at support) is not actionable regardless of shape.
risk_geometry: Not an entry by itself; upgrades the confidence/weight of a zone that then uses its own candle anchors for stops and targets; the 'cluster' technique (e.g., four bearish signals stacked at $38-$39.50 resistance) is the canonical example.
quote: I define convergence as 'a cluster of technical signals converging at, or near, the same price.' Convergence is a pivotal concept. This is because the more signals that join at a support or resistance area, the more likely a reversal.
chapter_anchor: Part 2 introduction and Chapter 10, A Cluster of Candles, pp. 181-191
notes: Central Part 2 thesis: candle signals are confirmatory, not standalone; 'where' a signal forms outweighs 'what' it is. For V8 this is a methodology lesson on the feature side (location/context weighting of CandidateDrafts) and a design note that single-family drafts should be context-weighted - a lab/registry question, not an expert behavior. Also the book's repeated 'candles give no price targets' point justifies pairing candle signals with Western targets.

strategy_name: Measured-move price targets used for exits only
mechanism: Western measured objectives (box height, flagpole, triangle height) forecast reversal extent; they offset existing positions, never initiate new ones
setup_summary: Compute a measured objective from a completed Western pattern (box breakout, swing target, flag/pennant flagpole, triangle height) and use it to exit or trim an existing position. A price target is not synonymous with support/resistance, does not guarantee the price will stop there, and does not predict the extent of a reversal.
trigger_invalidation: N/A — an exit methodology, not an entry trigger. Reaching a target does not justify a counter-position without independent reversal confirmation.
risk_geometry: Target-based exit: box-height/flagpole/triangle-height projected from the broken level; conservative variant projects flag objectives from the bottom of the flag rather than the top ('I prefer to err on exiting too early').
quote: one should not look at a price objective to initiate a new position, but to offset an outstanding position.

notes: Directly informs V8 risk_geometry target semantics: measured objectives are exits, and target != level (no auto-fade at target). Reinforces that stops and dead-thesis are distinct exits in the lifecycle.

strategy_name: Signal convergence at a price level strengthens reversal calls
mechanism: multiple independent signal families (candles + Western) converging in a narrow price zone raise the probability of a reversal; convergence does not project the extent of the move
setup_summary: A reversal is more credible when several independent signals cluster in the same price area. Example: shooting star + bearish engulfing + falling window + high-wave candle + rising resistance line + oscillator divergence all converging in one zone called a major NASDAQ top. Candles frequently give the turning signal ahead of Western indicators (dark-cloud cover preceded MACD reversal by almost a week).
trigger_invalidation: Confidence is graded by how many independent families agree at the same level; no single-family signal is sufficient on its own, and even strong convergence does not forecast correction depth.
risk_geometry: No standalone risk geometry; informs confirmation strength for other families.

strategy_name: Close-based confirmation for reversal candles and S/R levels
mechanism: reversal candle signals require a close-based confirmation bar; support/resistance is defined by closes, not intraday extremes
setup_summary: Hanging man requires a close under its real body the next session for bearish confirmation; inverted hammer requires a higher open and especially a higher close. Pattern-derived resistance/support holds on closes: pushing above an evening star's resistance intraday without closing above it leaves the level intact. A doji confirming hesitation needs a close under the nearby window to damage the trend.
trigger_invalidation: A candle signal without close-based confirmation is not actionable; an intraday tag of a level without a close-through is not a break.
risk_geometry: The confirmation bar defines the entry reference and the invalidation level (e.g., close under the hammer's low voids the bullish stochastic read).

strategy_name: Assumption-invalidation lifecycle exit ('if you are wrong, get out')
mechanism: every trade is a bundle of forecast assumptions; when any one is falsified by price, the position is dead and must be liquidated immediately
setup_summary: Lifecycle rule: plan exits for every assumption BEFORE entry (direction, magnitude, volatility behavior, timing - 'what does one do if he is completely wrong on direction? what if volatility behavior... turn out to be incorrect?'). If any assumption proves wrong, liquidate immediately; no hoping or praying, and avoid the classic error of staying too long or over-modifying a position whose view has changed.

strategy_name: Correlation Cap and Long/Short Unit Netting
mechanism: Correlated markets act as one big position; capping per-market units and netting long vs short units keeps true portfolio risk at the intended level.
setup_summary: Limit 4-5 units in any one market and avoid stacking highly correlated markets (gold+silver, Dow+S&P count as one position). Total portfolio unit risk is computed as larger − (smaller/2) between long and short unit totals, which allows more units overall while keeping risk constant.

mechanism: Trade payoff is determined primarily by the exit/liquidation criterion; entry has little information value once risk is controlled, so effort should go into exit design, not entry precision.

strategy_name: Ruin-avoidance bet-size cap ('never bet the ranch')
mechanism: Even with positive expectation, a position sized so a tail loss zeroes the account is unacceptable; the utility cost of ruin outweighs any edge.
setup_summary: For any candidate trade with win-probability p and a full-stake loss on failure, refuse stake sizes that can wipe out equity regardless of edge (Abraham's coin-flip: 90% chance to double $10M, 10% chance to lose all -> still must decline). Standing constraint on per-trade and portfolio risk.

strategy_name: Tail-event protection ('what can never happen can happen')
mechanism: tail_risk_conservatism: markets occasionally print multi-standard-deviation moves (Eurodollar +250 = ~10+ sigma in Oct 1987); stops and sizing must assume such moves occur intraday.

Simulator must model gap-through-stop fills, not just next-bar-close fills.
